articles.title: US Drugmakers Are Dependent on Chinese Supply Chains
articles.full_text:
Analysts warn a disruption in Chinese sources of common antibiotics or blood thinners could leave American patients with no reliable alternative.
China controls the upstream production chemistry for many of the most widely used generic drugs in the United States, leaving few backup suppliers if that access were disrupted, according to a recent report by former U.S. government officials. The vulnerability is drawing fresh attention as Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to travel to Washington, D.C. for a state visit on September 24, the first trip by a Chinese leader to the U.S. capital in more than a decade.
American and Chinese officials have spent recent weeks preparing for the visit, and artificial intelligence and trade friction are expected to dominate the agenda. Still, pharmaceutical dependence carries the same kind of coercive potential Beijing has shown in other sectors, and it touches medicines that tens of millions of Americans take every week.
Beijing has used that kind of leverage before. It restricted rare-earth exports to Japan during a 2010 territorial dispute, imposed trade barriers on Australian barley and wine after Canberra called for a COVID-19 origins inquiry, and curtailed trade with Lithuania after Vilnius opened a Taiwanese representative office. In none of those cases did Chinese officials announce the move or explain the reasoning beforehand.
According to the recent report published on September 2 by Scalare Advisors, a consultancy based in Washington, D.C., China supplied more than 70 percent of the antibiotic active ingredients by volume imported into the United States in 2024, and three of the most commonly used outpatient antibiotic drugs – amoxicillin, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin – all depend on Chinese-made ingredients. A simultaneous disruption in all three would leave doctors with no reliable outpatient antibiotic option that could be obtained at the necessary scale and speed.
One Chinese conglomerate, CSPC Pharmaceutical Group, produces both amoxicillin and azithromycin for the U.S. market, meaning a single company controls the fermentation-to-tablet chain for two of the three dominant outpatient antibiotic drugs. No equivalent domestic or allied producer exists for either drug.
Bristol-Myers Squibb announced the closure of its last U.S. penicillin fermentation plant in 2004 and ended production there the following year, eliminating domestic manufacturing of 6-aminopenicillanic acid, the building block for the penicillin-class drugs used to treat strep throat, ear infections, pneumonia, and Lyme disease. Today, no U.S. plant produces penicillin from scratch. This decision conceded penicillin production to China, which now makes about 90 percent of that ingredient worldwide.
Heparin – one of the most commonly used blood thinners – illustrates the same pattern. Pfizer has one heparin injection product on an active shortage list maintained by the Food and Drug Administration. The two remaining U.S.-based producers of the raw ingredient used to make it – Scientific Protein Laboratories in Wisconsin and Smithfield BioScience in Ohio – are both now owned by Chinese parent companies. The broader supply of crude heparin traces back to China, leaving roughly 550,000 Americans who rely on the anticoagulant for dialysis with no clinical substitute if that supply were interrupted.
Hydrocortisone, a prescription drug essential for treating inflammation, is manufactured by Pfizer in Michigan but still depends on a Chinese supplier – a state-owned enterprise named Tianjin Tianyao Pharmaceuticals – for the drug’s active ingredients, according to the same review of federal drug-safety programs. The FDA detected hydrogen cyanide contamination in active ingredient shipments from Tianjin Tianyao Pharmaceuticals in December 2015, following a chemical warehouse explosion in August of that same year. If the FDA had not caught the tainted ingredients, it would have triggered a public health crisis in the United States.
This has happened before. Back in 2008, contaminated heparin traced to a supplier in China killed at least 149 Americans. At the time, Chinese officials denied that the contamination originated there and refused U.S. federal investigators access to conduct a criminal inquiry.
Industrial policy in Beijing adds a different type of risk. The 15th Five-Year Plan, issued in March, named biomanufacturing as one of the sectors targeted for “decisive breakthroughs.” An industry analysis published in May found that the number of product categories in which China held a dominant market position rose from 192 in 2021 to 315 in 2024.
Analysts increasingly view China’s dominance in supply chains as a national security threat, rather than a purely economic one. The concentration of drug manufacturing in China means that decisions made in Beijing shape whether American hospitals can fill a prescription.
Experts also point to the drug manufacturers’ lack of transparency about their supply chain exposures to potentially hostile markets like China. Currently, there is little U.S. federal regulation that requires these companies to publicly disclose the origins of active pharmaceutical ingredients or key starting materials of their products. Experts agree that both relevant agencies and the pharmaceutical industry should be held more accountable to make this information more transparent, especially as these market exposures increasingly become national security concerns.
Washington has confirmed the September 24 date for Xi’s state visit, and U.S. and Chinese trade officials held a video call in July to prepare for the visit. Neither government has signaled that pharmaceutical supply chains will be part of the formal agenda, yet the medicines Americans use every day are intrinsically linked to the broader China-U.S. relationship, whether or not they are named in a joint statement.

articles.title: Mongolia’s President at the SCO Summit
articles.full_text:
For Mongolia, the highlights were the bilateral meetings held on the sidelines with Kyrgyzstan, China, and Russia.
Mongolia’s President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa stands alongside other SCO heads of state in preparation for a group photo during the 2026 Bishkek Summit, Sep. 1, 2026.
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa is attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of State in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan as the organization recognizes its 25th anniversary. While the SCO spent much of its existence focused on security and regional cooperation, the Bishkek Declaration demonstrates a much larger global agenda. Mongolia, in the new partner state status, is seeking deeper ties with SCO member states in emerging sectors via robust bilateral links.
For example, Khurelsukh and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, the summit’s host, held bilateral talks to accelerate political, economic, and trade relations under the Comprehensive Partnership Agreement that was signed during Khurelsukh’s state visit to Bishkek in 2025.  
Mongolia and Kyrgyzstan are aiming to boost regional trade turnover to $100 million. During Khurelsukh’s remarks, he noted the trade volume between the two countries had grown from $2.6 million in 2023 to $19 million as of 2025. The Mongolian side expressed interest in further Kyrgyz investments and joint projects in developing industries, minerals exploration, transport and logistics, and direct flights. 
Mongolia’s interim free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) creates additional trade opportunities for the two countries. Kyrgyzstan will be chairing the EAEU in 2027.
But there were more leaders in Bishkek than just Japarov. For Mongolia, the SCO Summit was a valuable opportunity for face-to-face diplomacy as the world faces major geopolitical and economic challenges. 
On August 31, Khurelsukh held bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. During their meeting, Xi reiterated Beijing’s long-term support for Mongolia as close neighbors and promised to support “win-win cooperation.” 
Mongolia and China discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in emerging sectors such as green minerals, AI, digital economy, and supporting Mongolia’s efforts in combating desertification and climate issues. According to the Mongolian presidential office, Khurelsukh and Xi discussed several projects that are underway, including China’s support for the operation of the Erdeneburen Hydropower Plant, a long-stalled mega-project that received new life in 2022.
Xi and Khurelsukh also discussed the need to make progress on constructing the Shiveekhuren-Sekhee, Bichigt-Zuunkhatavch, Khangi-Mandal railways which are crucial to the countries’ bilateral economic activities.
Moreover, one of the most important discussion points was China’s willingness to continue exporting petroleum product supplies to Mongolia amid fuel shortages triggered by supply disruptions from Russia. The two sides are currently aiming for Mongolia to import 71,000 tons of petroleum product per month from China. 
More broadly, Xi promised to support Mongolia’s fuel industry, and cooperate in the exploration of oil and gas, a key priority for Mongolia as it seeks to address its energy dependencies. 
While China is a leading investor in Mongolia’s mining sector, it has yet to allocate investments into the renewable energy sector. Considering Mongolia’s push to transition to renewable energy and diversify its energy sources, Beijing’s contribution will be crucial in the coming years. 
Khurelsukh also met with Russian President Vladimir Putin while in Bishkek. During the meeting, Putin reiterated the historic links between Mongolia and Russia. He expressed hope that Ulaanbaatar’s interim free trade agreement with the EAEU will provide “preferential treatment for Mongolian traditional exports across the customs territory of our association.” 
Moreover, Putin highlighted that Mongolia – previously an observer in the SCO – now will receive “partner state” status. Last year, the SCO streamlined its various levels of participation to just two: full members and partner states. Mongolia thus became a partner state along with other states previously recognized as observer states. The debate on whether Mongolia should join the SCO as a full member has been a hot topic among scholars and policymakers in the last decade. 
The Khurelsukh-Putin summit was also attended by the Russian energy minister and president of Rosatom, Russia’s nuclear power corporation. Rosatom’s leader reportedly met with Mongolian partners to discuss small modular nuclear reactors as a way to diversify Mongolia’s energy mix.
According to Russia’s Pivot to Asia official website, “Mongolia is reviewing a proposal from the Russian state nuclear corporation to build a small modular nuclear reactor in the country, which may be built near New Kharkhorum, a planned new capital city located about 230 kilometers west of Ulaanbaatar.”
Following Khurelsukh’s high-level meetings with both Xi and Putin, separately, Xi and Putin resumed high-stakes negotiations on the construction of Power of Siberia 2, a long-discussed gas pipeline that would bring LNG from Russia’s Yamal gas fields to China via Mongolia.  
According to Pipeline Technology Journal, “Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov confirmed Friday that the flagship energy project will feature prominently during talks in Bishkek.” Ushakov added that discussions will continue at the Eastern Economic Forum currently underway in Vladivostok, where Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang will meet with Russian officials. 
Russia is keen to export more gas to China, and Mongolia has welcomed the construction of the pipeline. However, China has been driving a hard bargain on pricing, especially as it moves away from fossil fuels toward renewable energy.
There was no China-Mongolia-Russia trilateral meeting scheduled in Bishkek. However, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor is in Vladivostok through September 4, so trilateral talks might be resumed there. 
The three heads of state gathered last year in Beijing shortly after the 2025 SCO summit in nearby Tianjin. At that meeting, Mongolia emphasized the importance of trilateral cooperation and reaffirmed its commitment to jointly implementing the projects and programs outlined in the Economic Corridor Construction Program. 
As evidenced by the Bishkek Declaration, the SCO is setting itself up as a much larger player in global political, economic, and security arenas. As SCO member states encompass approximately 42 percent of the global population, SCO-linked global governance, multipolarity, and economic and trade are set to expand in the organization’s next 25 years. 
While Mongolia’s participation in this year’s SCO in Bishkek has been primarily economically motivated, Ulaanbaatar is aware of the shifts in global geopolitics. Mongolia engagement in the SCO is underpinned by its bilateral relationships: comprehensive strategic partnerships with Russia, China, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan, coupled with strategic partnership frameworks with other SCO members such as India and Kazakhstan. In all of these relationship, Mongolia envisions greater cooperation in emerging critical sectors and seeks to strengthen the country’s political, economic, and cultural capital. Ulaanbaatar can achieve that through robust bilateral links without having to a commit to the SCO as an organization.

articles.title: From Partnership to Penalty: US Tariffs Shadow India Trade Deal
articles.full_text:
The promise of deeper economic cooperation is undermined by punitive measures that could torpedo the India-U.S. pact even before it is signed.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with U.S. President Donald Trump in happier times at the White House, June 26, 2017.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor recently claimed that the India-U.S. trade agreement is on the verge of finalization and that “almost everything” about the agreement was done “in principle.” 
However, even as Gor was exuding confidence regarding the deal, two initiatives taken in Washington in just over a month have brought yet another round of the tariff war to India’s doorstep. These initiatives have the potential of increasing friction between the two countries, and could even torpedo the deal. 
The most egregious of these developments is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a bipartisan bill proposed in the U.S. Senate, which has the backing of the U.S. President Donald Trump. 
The second development is Trump’s proposal to impose 100 percent tariffs on generic medicines from 2028, unless the firms exporting these medicines do not reshore their operations to the U.S. This proposal could significantly affect India’s pharmaceutical industry since the U.S. is its largest export market.
The bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named after the late Republican senator, who was the bill’s strongest proponent, was overwhelmingly voted by the Senate (86-11) in early August. The House of Representatives will take up the bill for consideration after it reconvenes in early September, and could push for its early adoption.
The primary objective of the bill is to tighten the economic sanctions on Russia for its continued war on Ukraine. The bill proposes 500 percent tariffs on all goods imported into the U.S. from Russia. It also proposes 100 percent tariffs on all goods imported into the U.S. from the five largest importers of crude oil or natural gas, by total volume, originating in the Russian Federation. As one of the largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil, India also faces penal tariffs for facilitating Russia’s sanctions evasion.
Market analysts put India as the second-largest buyer of Russian crude oil in July 2026, valued at over $7.3 billion, or about 37 percent of Russia’s global exports.  
According to Indian government data, India’s dependence on Russian crude oil increased from 30 percent to nearly 43 percent of its total imports between January and June 2026. In February 2026, after the U.S. and India reached a framework for an interim agreement as a step toward finalizing the trade deal, Trump announced that the 25 percent tariffs imposed on India in August 2025 for importing Russian crude oil was withdrawn. 
India, according to Trump, had “committed to stop directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil, has represented that it will purchase United States energy products from the United States.”
However, after the conflict in West Asia, India’s dependence on Russian crude increased to record levels, and simultaneously, its imports from the U.S. dropped from 13 percent in April 2025 to three percent in June 2026. Trump would surely have viewed this development as a trigger for action against India.
India’s generic pharmaceutical industry faces uncertain times following Trump’s post on Truth Social announcing his decision to impose a 100 percent tariff on all generic medicines from 2028,  and increased to 200 percent a year by 2029. The objective of this proposed increase in tariffs is to “Reshore Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America, with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time given to them.”
This announcement followed an earlier decision by Trump to impose a 100 percent tariff on patented pharmaceuticals and associated pharmaceutical ingredients from July 31, 2026, if the companies exporting them do not declare plans to start producing in the US. Thus, Trump has put in place an expansive plan to control the global pharmaceutical industry. 
Pharmaceuticals are the second largest products in India’s export basket to the U.S., accounting for about 13 percent of total exports in 2025-26. More importantly, the U.S. is the largest export market for all major Indian pharmaceutical companies. 
The U.S. accounted for about a third of the total sales of most companies, but two Indian pharma companies — Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories and Zydus Life Sciences — are considerably more dependent on the US market: their shares of sales to the US were close to  50 percent in 2023-24. 
Besides, all the top Indian companies have invested in production capacities in the U.S. through their subsidiaries, with the largest company, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries having 21 subsidiaries in 2025-26. 
Trump’s insistence that the generic pharmaceutical companies must invest in the US to escape 100 percent tariff in 2028 has had its desired effect as  Indian companies, including pharmaceutical companies have already announced their plans to invest over  $19.1 billion to increase their production capacities in the US. 
Only time will tell whether these investments will result in diversion of India’s domestic pharmaceutical production to the U.S., and the implication this could have on the availability of medicines in India.

articles.title: Prioritizing Social Stability Over Democratic Reforms: Uzbekistan Announces New Development Programs
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan’s new national development programs prioritize socio-economic developments over democratic reforms.
As Uzbekistan celebrated its 35th independence anniversary this week, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced seven national programs for the years ahead. The programs focus on socio-economic development and conspicuously omit any reform related to political pluralism, press freedom, freedom of conscience, or other democratic elements. 
Mirziyoyev has prioritized areas viewed as critical to retaining popular support for his government. The first is improving public education, with a special focus on extending compulsory education to age six, supporting private kindergartens, and having at least ten universities ranked in the top 1,000 higher education institutions in the world. Uzbekistan has one of the highest numbers of schoolchildren in the region, with 6.8 million students and 600,000 teachers in public mandatory schools alone. 
The next few national programs announced by Mirziyoyev also concern socio-economic well-being: improving public health and increasing longevity; transitioning to a high technology economy, and ensuring high labor productivity as well as changing public attitudes toward the environment and addressing environmental challenges. 
The fifth national program is set to ensure judicial independence and the rule of law. The Diplomat recently reported that one of the country’s new laws allows the president’s daughter, who heads the presidential administration, to be directly involved in shaping the judicial system while having lifetime legal immunity for her actions with no accountability. A few areas – cybercrime, drug trafficking, and human trafficking – are singled out for additional attention but concrete steps in this regard have not been outlined.
The sixth program Mirziyoyev announced identified mahallas as the “‘main customer (or commissioner)’ of development.” This program basically aims to further empower mahallas along with slightly altering the district budgeting system. Mahallas are unique self-governing institutions established at the neighborhood level. Each household is part of a mahalla. As of 2021, there were 9,251 mahallas across the country. 
“The mood of our people, the well-being of families, the dreams and aspirations of young people, and the initiative of entrepreneurs are first and foremost reflected in the neighborhood,” Mirziyoyev said in his speech. “Mood” is an odd word to pick – not financial stability, safety, employment or other aspects of socio-economic life. It reflects mahallas’ role as an observer of citizens’ sentiment (and hopefully their needs too). 
Historically, mahalla institutions have played a distributing role rather than a commissioning one, carrying government policies down and out to the people rather than gathering and feeding social sentiments upward into the system. Mirziyoyev is now saying that mahallas ought to be “the main customer (commissioner) of social development.” While this is, in one sense, a form of decentralization where citizens might participate in some degree of decision-making, it is not a genuine political decentralization. It appears that mahallas will report upward the social and financial needs on the ground and the budget allocation will be made accordingly. The president’s announcement noted, “District budgets, investment programs, and infrastructure projects are developed based on the needs of neighborhoods.” 
But mahallas still will not have a final say in anything. They will not receive full control over their own budgets. Ultimate decisions on budget allocations will remain at the hands of the central government. The proposed change, if implemented, will result in participatory or needs-based local governance, but does not grant fiscal independence. 
The last area of development focuses on a peaceful foreign policy and economic diplomacy.
The proposed national development programs place emphasis on socio-economic areas. These are safe areas wherein changes, minor or even radical, will not threaten or challenge the political regime. Instead, increased attention to these spheres will increase Mirziyoyev’s popularity and thus further consolidate power in the existing government. 
The programs as outlined do not address areas in which Mirziyoyev initially promised reforms, particularly freedom of expression. His early promises on supporting journalists and allowing the press to become a true watchdog has undergone a clear backslide. The Diplomat has continuously reported on waves of arrests of local bloggers, including popular religious scholar and blogger, Mubashshir Ahmad. Not only journalists or bloggers, but ordinary citizens are also regularly charged with crimes and sentenced to prison for expressing their personal religious views, sharing religious songs online that are not approved by the government or for saying anything negative about the president or his family. The recent law that expanded the authority of the presidential administration,  headed by Mirziyoyev’s first daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, also prohibits “insulting the honor and dignity” of its officials. The law does not explicitly differentiate between healthy criticism and insult. 
The Mirziyoyev administration’s priorities are clear in its announced programs: to keep average people happy by ensuring their basic needs are covered. Anything else, particularly those related to freedom of speech, mobilization, or independent teaching and practice of religion that can eventually challenge the status quo, has been swept under the carpet.

The sixth program Mirziyoyev announced identified mahallas as the “‘main customer (or commissioner)’ of development.” This program basically aims to further empower mahallas along with slightly altering the district budgeting system. Mahallas are unique self-governing institutions established at the neighborhood level. Each household is part of a mahalla. As of 2021, there were 9,251 mahallas across the country. 
“The mood of our people, the well-being of families, the dreams and aspirations of young people, and the initiative of entrepreneurs are first and foremost reflected in the neighborhood,” Mirziyoyev said in his speech. “Mood” is an odd word to pick – not financial stability, safety, employment or other aspects of socio-economic life. It reflects mahallas’ role as an observer of citizens’ sentiment (and hopefully their needs too). 
Historically, mahalla institutions have played a distributing role rather than a commissioning one, carrying government policies down and out to the people rather than gathering and feeding social sentiments upward into the system. Mirziyoyev is now saying that mahallas ought to be “the main customer (commissioner) of social development.” While this is, in one sense, a form of decentralization where citizens might participate in some degree of decision-making, it is not a genuine political decentralization. It appears that mahallas will report upward the social and financial needs on the ground and the budget allocation will be made accordingly. The president’s announcement noted, “District budgets, investment programs, and infrastructure projects are developed based on the needs of neighborhoods.” 
But mahallas still will not have a final say in anything. They will not receive full control over their own budgets. Ultimate decisions on budget allocations will remain at the hands of the central government. The proposed change, if implemented, will result in participatory or needs-based local governance, but does not grant fiscal independence. 
The last area of development focuses on a peaceful foreign policy and economic diplomacy.
The proposed national development programs place emphasis on socio-economic areas. These are safe areas wherein changes, minor or even radical, will not threaten or challenge the political regime. Instead, increased attention to these spheres will increase Mirziyoyev’s popularity and thus further consolidate power in the existing government. 
The programs as outlined do not address areas in which Mirziyoyev initially promised reforms, particularly freedom of expression. His early promises on supporting journalists and allowing the press to become a true watchdog has undergone a clear backslide. The Diplomat has continuously reported on waves of arrests of local bloggers, including popular religious scholar and blogger, Mubashshir Ahmad. Not only journalists or bloggers, but ordinary citizens are also regularly charged with crimes and sentenced to prison for expressing their personal religious views, sharing religious songs online that are not approved by the government or for saying anything negative about the president or his family. The recent law that expanded the authority of the presidential administration,  headed by Mirziyoyev’s first daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, also prohibits “insulting the honor and dignity” of its officials. The law does not explicitly differentiate between healthy criticism and insult. 
The Mirziyoyev administration’s priorities are clear in its announced programs: to keep average people happy by ensuring their basic needs are covered. Anything else, particularly those related to freedom of speech, mobilization, or independent teaching and practice of religion that can eventually challenge the status quo, has been swept under the carpet.
As Uzbekistan celebrated its 35th independence anniversary this week, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced seven national programs for the years ahead. The programs focus on socio-economic development and conspicuously omit any reform related to political pluralism, press freedom, freedom of conscience, or other democratic elements. 
Mirziyoyev has prioritized areas viewed as critical to retaining popular support for his government. The first is improving public education, with a special focus on extending compulsory education to age six, supporting private kindergartens, and having at least ten universities ranked in the top 1,000 higher education institutions in the world. Uzbekistan has one of the highest numbers of schoolchildren in the region, with 6.8 million students and 600,000 teachers in public mandatory schools alone. 
Aziz Adilov is a pseudonym for a journalist based in Uzbekistan.
articles.summary: Uzbekistan’s new national development programs prioritize socio-economic developments over democratic reforms.

articles.title: Land Seizures in the Name of Development in Vietnam
articles.full_text:
More and more Vietnamese are being forcibly displaced to make way for development. Many are reluctant to speak out, because “between a victim and a criminal lies only a fragile line.”
A plot of land in Hanoi under construction after the site was cleared.
Born into a family with a passion for the arts, 68-year-old Thanh spent her younger years enjoying stage dramas at Hanoi’s theaters in the 1980s. Such entertainment was a luxury in post-war Vietnam – theater tickets were scarce, accessible only to families with wealth or political connections. Thanh was among the fortunate few.
Today, however, she views the imminent $520 million Pearl Theater with bitterness. The megaproject – covering a total floor area of 40,980 square meters and potentially accommodating 2,000 people – is slated for completion by 2030. But the giant theater’s construction displaced her whole neighborhood. 
“I lost my home,” Thanh said in her trembling voice. 
She spent the past weeks inviting friends and family to her two-story house, a 230-square-meter property near West Lake that she completed in 2020, for what may be their last visit. The house, valued at over 300 billion Vietnamese dong (around $11.5 million) in the current market, was demolished at the end of August.
The compensation she received was 3 billion dong – just 1 percent of her home’s estimated valued – plus a monthly allowance that is barely enough for a modest rent. The financial toll extends beyond the compensation gap. Thanh and her neighbors have spent considerable time and money petitioning local authorities, along with paying unofficial fees to expedite bureaucratic processes – efforts that yielded no concessions. 
Authorities have designated resettlement areas for Thanh and her neighbors but they remain far from ready to move. Thanh has scrambled for months to secure alternative housing for her family of seven, unsure when she will officially move to the resettlement residential areas. 
Nonetheless, Thanh refuses to join any protest with some of her neighbors nor air her discontent online, though she is an active user of Facebook and Zalo, a local messaging application.  
“Nowadays, between a victim and a criminal lies only a fragile line,” said Thanh. “We have to be careful.”
Thanh is not alone in facing the dilemma brought about by the capital’s 100-year multibillion dollar master plan, which is poised to displace 860,000 people or more than 10 percent of the capital’s population. The haste to demolish hits the communities hard. 
Thanh said she and her neighbors were never consulted during planning and were coerced to leave their homes without access to resettlement areas – and, most importantly, received inadequate compensation. To make matters worse, authorities are forcibly accelerating displacement even as resettlement infrastructure remains unfinished. 
Yet, this practice is bound to gain legal sanction in the upcoming amended Land Law. On July 28, the National Assembly’s Standing Committee announced that an extraordinary session would be held in August to deliberate on several draft laws. Among those high on the agenda is the amended Land Law, which is scheduled for approval in October.
Since To Lam became chief of the Communist Party of Vietnam in 2025 – and, in 2026, president – the slogan of the “era of national rise” has become a mantra across Vietnam. Much of this agenda revolves around a money-driven model of development: policymakers pursue double-digit GDP growth and the ambition of transforming Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Land, in particular, has been seen as a launching pad for national growth. Large-scale real estate developments continue to proliferate across the country. 
Amid the rush to develop, one of the government’s most aggressively pursued – yet quietly contested – initiatives in recent months has been land confiscation. 
Land Rights at the Mercy of the Party-State
The draft legislation, prepared by the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, was released for public consultation on July 21, leaving citizens less than a month to submit feedback – assuming they were even aware that the consultation was taking place. Notably, on the online portal to provide input, there is no option to do so anonymously.  
The Land Law was passed two years ago, so it’s surprising that it already needs amendments – despite the fact that in 2024 and 2025, two resolutions were issued to guide its implementation. But in today’s Vietnam, laws are being issued with unprecedented speed and scale. 2025 was a record legislative year, with 86 laws passed – more than half of the 150 total laws approved by the National Assembly from 2021 to 2026 – as well as 371 legal documents of varying types. 
China and Vietnam share a socialist land-tenure system that does not recognize private land ownership. But their legal ownership structures differ. In China, urban land is state-owned, while most rural land is owned by peasant collectives. In Vietnam, all land is legally owned by the entire people, with the state acting as the representative and granting land-use rights to individuals, households, and organizations – and reclaiming those rights when it sees fit.
Hanoi is currently carrying out land acquisition and site clearance for 1,428 projects across the city. According to a master plan approved in March 2026, Hanoi has set a goal becoming one of the 10 happiest capitals in the world, a city of “prosperity, harmony, civility, and character.” Yet, experts inside the country has expressed concerns about the speed of the transformation.
Tô Kiên, an architect and professor at the University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City, wrote in an opinion piece on Vnexxpress: 
The Hanoi master plan was meticulously prepared, comprising more than 1,000 pages of explanatory documents and dozens of large-scale maps. Yet the public was given only 10 days to become aware of it, read and understand it, and provide feedback. Expert consultation workshops had only just taken place, and within days, the plan was approved. This shows that the consultation process has not fulfilled its intended role and should have been conducted more thoroughly and cautiously, with more time allowed for review and feedback.
The 12th and 13th provisions of the current Land Law allow the state to expropriate land to build headquarters for the Communist Party of Vietnam, state agencies, the Vietnam Fatherland Front, political and socio-political organizations, and other organizations established in accordance with the law and assigned state functions. They also allow land to be expropriated to build offices or representative offices for public service units affiliated with CPV agencies, state agencies, and socio-political organizations.
The final provision goes further. It states that if land must be expropriated for a project or facility deemed to serve the national or public interest but does not fall under any of the 33 categories listed in the article, the National Assembly may amend or supplement the list through a simplified legislative procedure. In practice, this could leave the door open for the state to add new grounds for land expropriation through an expedited process. 
It also raises questions about how much say affected communities will have over whether – and under what circumstances – their land can be taken. The provisions appear to prioritize the interests of state and party institutions over those of land users when it comes to determining which projects qualify for compulsory land acquisition.
Since mid-2025, large-scale land acquisition and forced eviction in the name of “development and investment” has been and is being carried out nationwide, pushing hundreds of thousands of households into situations where they lose their homes and land. The Red River Scenic Avenue Corridor Project runs through 16 communes and wards, with a total land area of about 11,418 hectares, potentially affecting approximately 200,000 residents. The Gia Bình International Airport Project in Bắc Ninh province will require nearly 1,960 hectares of land, affecting about 7,100 households and 118 organizations. The Long Thành Airport Project in Đồng Nai province will need about 5,000 hectares, affecting 4,600 households.
Like China, peaceful peasant protests over land expropriation in Vietnam first began to take shape in the early 2000s, and became widespread and more significant in the mid-2000s. In Vietnam today, approximately 70 percent of long-term citizen complaints, denunciations, and lawsuits derive from state land acquisition, site clearance, compensation, and management.
While Article 158 of the Land Law states that land pricing must follow market principles and be honest, objective, and transparent, in practice the terms are effectively imposed by local authorities rather than subject to negotiation.
In the eyes of the state, protesting the terms of land expropriation is criminal activity. Domestic media outlets warn citizens that stories shedding light on victims’ struggles are being used by “hostile and reactionary forces” to spread false information, incite opposition, sow divisions between the public and the authorities, and portray the implementation of the project as “driving people away, suppressing them, and abandoning them.” The newly elected National Assembly is silent on the struggles of forced evictees. Speaking out on behalf of them was already rare in the past, but it did happen previously
Lưu Bình Nhưỡng, a senior CPV member, and former member of Vietnam’s 14th National Assembly (2016–2021), was among the most vocal legislators on the issue of land confiscation. From 2021 to 2023, he was the deputy head of the Commission for Members’ Opinions and Petitions under the Standing Committee of the National Assembly.
articles.summary: More and more Vietnamese are being forcibly displaced to make way for development. Many are reluctant to speak out, because “between a victim and a criminal lies only a fragile line.”

articles.title: Balancing China and Russia: India’s Tightrope Walk at BRICS
articles.full_text:
New Delhi aims to keep BRICS relevant to the Global South while preventing its transformation into a Chinese bandwagon or an explicitly anti-Western coalition.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the SCO summit in Tianjin, China, September 1, 2025.
On August 28, at the end of the 25th round of special representative level talks between India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing, both sides separately issued an eight-point list of outcomes and consensus that promises to advance the future dialogue on the vexed boundary issue. Regardless of ultimate resolution, the outcome laid the groundwork for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s anticipated visit to New Delhi to attend the 18th BRICS summit on September 12 and 13. 
India is currently the BRICS chair. Although still unconfirmed, this would be Xi’s first visit to India in seven years. He and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are expected to hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit to add momentum to their continued effort to rebuild the frayed China-India ties. 
Both leaders attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, August 31 to September 1. However, no bilateral exchanges were held, barring a handshake between the two that lasted few seconds. New Delhi prefers the venue for a high-profile meeting to be inside the country, not at a foreign location or for mere optics. 
Russian President Vladimir Putin also attended the SCO summit in Bishkek and will also travel to New Delhi for the BRICS summit later in September. Bishkek was the venue for an official Modi-Putin meeting on August 31, where both leaders discussed various key aspects of bilateral ties, including cooperation in areas of trade and investment, energy, and defense. Modi reportedly offered Putin India’s mediation assistance in ending the war with Ukraine. They also shared a car to travel to the opening ceremony for the World Nomad Games, currently underway in Kyrgyzstan. Notably, Putin met Xi for a bilateral meeting in Bishkek also. 
No such meeting between Putin and Modi, however, has been planned in New Delhi. India seems to be heavily invested on ensuring a productive meeting with the Chinese, undiluted by any other high-profile engagement. While this urgency by New Delhi and Beijing to manage their relationship is shaped by evolving geopolitics, the meetings, their venues, and agendas are part of the broader power flexing, hedging, and ally hunting that has marked the existence and workings of BRICS in the last two decades. 
One of the core principles of the inception, working, and expansion of minilateral organizations is internal cohesion. A common vision unites members. While differences and their explicit articulation are common in the larger universal forums and multilateral organizations such as the United Nations, minilateral groups are built to espouse specific goals, and their success depends on the extent to which differences are kept manageable or outside the agenda of the organization. 
BRICS stands apart in this respect, particularly given the constant power play and maneuverings between the three leading members: India, China, and Russia. The trajectory of the bilateral relationship between India and China, on the one hand, and India and Russia, on the other, seems to be the two parallel yet connected tracks shaping how far New Delhi is willing to let the group’s agenda be framed as anti-Western. For example, principally due to New Delhi’s opposition, the de-dollarization campaign initiated by China and Russia has stalled. India does support the group’s alternative financial institutions, like the New Development Bank (NDB), which provides credit without conditionalities, unlike those imposed by Western institutions. It also uses bilateral local currency agreement such as the India-UAE Local Currency Settlement System (to trade in rupee and dirham) and digital frameworks like BRICS Pay to reduce vulnerability to sanctions, tariffs, and the volatility of the U.S. dollar.
New Delhi aims to achieve a range of objectives during its chairmanship, seeking to make the group more “ practical, actionable, development-oriented,” and responsive to the challenges confronting the Global South. It has sought to give the acronym BRICS itself a new policy meaning: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” advocating for “humanity first” and “people-centric” approach. However, the key to achieving even its rather less-contentious agenda – including issues such as disaster resilience, clean energy, climate action, green finance, energy transition, health, fintech, digital public infrastructure, AI, trade, supply chains resilience, and space economy – needs support from other members, including China and Russia. New Delhi’s parallel diplomacy in Beijing and Bishkek appears to be geared toward those ends.  
At the same time, though, the unresolved border dispute with China has cast a long shadow over India’s engagement with BRICS. New Delhi has consistently resisted efforts to expand the grouping’s economic or connectivity initiatives in ways that could indirectly legitimize Chinese infrastructure ambitions, such as linkages to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), which India opposes tooth and nail. India has also been opposed to proposals for a common BRICS currency, wary that such instruments could be dominated by Chinese financial architecture. Similarly, both Russia and China are open to Pakistan’s membership into BRICS, which New Delhi resists given its adversarial relationship with Pakistan and its apprehension of allowing the China-Pakistan axis a new platform. Pakistan’s fragile economic profile doesn’t qualify it to become a BRICS member, India has argued. Moreover, the internal fragmentation, differences, and dilution of agenda with the inclusion of new members like Egypt and Ethiopia, Iran, and UAE has made New Delhi cautious about inviting more new members. The bandwagoning of countries with China further compounded these complexities.
This underlying distrust means India often approaches BRICS summits with a defensive posture, prioritizing the containment of Chinese influence while pursuing ambitious collective goals. It is unlikely that even a successful Modi-Xi meeting will shift the pronounced lack of trust that characterizes relations between the two countries.
India’s relationship with Russia, on the other hand, has been forged over decades of defense cooperation, energy trade, and diplomatic support. It provides India a crucial counterbalance within BRICS. Russia remains one of India’s largest arms suppliers, and the relationship has only deepened since the Ukraine war pushed Moscow to provide discounted oil exports that New Delhi eagerly absorbs. 
In an ironic twist, India of late has emerged as a key supplier of gasoline to Russia, after large Russian refineries were crippled by Ukrainian attacks.  While this is unlikely to change the distorted trade between the two countries, such need-based partnership gives India a degree of comfort operating within the China-heavy grouping. 
Russian and Chinese ties are also complex, marked by mutual dependence, strategic mistrust, and competing interests. Yet both countries have increasingly found common ground in challenging the existing U.S.-led international order. India, on the other hand, frequently leverages its ties with Russia and, more importantly, the latter’s dependency on non-Western partners to ensure Moscow remains sensitive to Indian security and diplomatic concerns. India has supported Russian positions on issues where doing so does not conflict with its own strategic autonomy and the goal of building a multipolar world order. However, even this seemingly strong partnership has to navigate the largely anti-Western motives that Russia shares with China. 
These divergences and distrust will continue to test BRICS’ unity and growth potential. New Delhi aims to keep BRICS relevant to the Global South while preventing its transformation into a Chinese bandwagon or an explicitly anti-Western coalition. But detachment from Beijing isn’t an option. It requires a complex skill set and diplomatic dexterity of engaging China adequately, aligning with Russia tangentially, and at the same time maintaining India’s strategic autonomy. Ironically, these very bilateral relationships that make this balancing act possible also reveal the limitations of BRICS as a unified political project. Under the changing world order, for India, maintaining this balance may ultimately prove to be a more significant achievement than any ambitious new initiative announced during its chairmanship.

articles.title: The Limbang Question Lingers On
articles.full_text:
The territory’s curious status is the result of an unresolved border dispute between Malaysia and Brunei that dates back to the British colonial era.
A river in the district of Limbang, in Malaysia’s Sarawak state.
Whenever young Bruneians want to eat chicken wings and drink beer, they often head to Limbang in neighboring Malaysia. It may sound strange to cross an international border for an evening out, but Limbang is only a few kilometers from Brunei’s capital, Bandar Seri Begawan.
One might marvel at how, despite an unresolved border dispute in the area, the two countries allow their citizens to freely travel back and forth. But as part of ASEAN, Bruneians and Malaysians don’t need visas to cross the border.
Geography has also made this sleepy town something of a go-between for Brunei and Malaysia, especially when it comes to Temburong, Brunei’s eastern district. Many people living there travel daily to Bandar Seri Begawan for work, but the land route takes them through Limbang. In effect, to travel from one part of their own country to another, they enter Malaysia and then cross back into Brunei. Limbang residents face a similar peculiarity when traveling within Sarawak, of which Limbang is a part. To reach Miri, the nearest Sarawak city, they have to pass through Brunei before re-entering Sarawak to the west.
For a foreign traveler, the arrangement can be bewildering, as multiple border crossings and immigration stamps can quickly fill up their passports. For Bruneians and Malaysians, it is easier, as they can generally use their identity cards for cross-border travel.
Limbang’s curious status is the result of an unresolved border dispute that dates back to the British colonial era – a dispute that the two sides are now moving toward resolving. During the 27th Annual Leaders’ Consultation in Bandar Seri Begawan on August 21, Brunei’s Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim discussed the demarcation of the two countries’ land boundary. More than half of the border has now been demarcated. Yet the question of Limbang still lingers on.
In a joint communiqué issued after their meeting, the two leaders reaffirmed the 2009 Exchange of Letters, the March 2012 boundary memorandum and its Terms of Reference, collectively describing them as binding instruments. It also directs the two sides to resolve Sector F–G, which covers the Limbang area, solely through the watershed principle, using one jointly determined watershed, before completing the survey and demarcation by May 31, 2027.
According to senior Bruneian journalist Malai Hassan Othman, Sector F–G is supposed to cover roughly 6.6 kilometers from Bebuloh towards a point west of Bukit Gadong, near Kampong Limau Manis and the Kuala Lurah-Tedungan crossing (Kuala Lurah is the Brunei border checkpoint, and Tedungan is the matching Malaysian checkpoint in Sarawak for travel between Brunei and Limbang. It lies along the Brunei-Muara-Limbang frontier and is therefore geographically connected to Limbang. But it would be misleading to describe the sector as synonymous with the entire Limbang territorial question.
Malai Hassan, in an article published on LinkedIn, explained in detail the historical background of the sovereignty dispute over Limbang. Buttressing Brunei’s claim, he writes that records from 1970 clearly indicate that the late Sultan Haji Omar ’Ali Saifuddien, father of the present Sultan, stressed Brunei’s claim over Limbang.
Historically, Limbang was governed within the Brunei Sultanate and provided revenue, food, and river access to the sultanate. However, the Limbang Rebellion of 1884 was a crucial conflict between the Sultanate of Brunei and the indigenous residents of Limbang that led to the annexation of Limbang in March 1890 by Charles Brooke, the rajah of Sarawak. He claimed that local Limbang chiefs no longer wanted the Sultan’s rule and preferred Sarawak.
The British gave tacit and informal approval to the annexation of Limbang despite fierce protests from Sultan Hashim of Brunei.
Malai Hassan says that the Sultan rejected the proposed annual compensation, refusing to exchange territory for payment. Britain declared the matter closed in 1895, but that administrative decision did not secure Brunei’s agreement.
This split Brunei into two parts, and Temburong was separated from the other districts of Brunei.
The most serious attempt to resolve the issue came in 2009, when the Exchange of Letters was signed by the Brunei Sultan and then Malaysian Prime Minister Abdullah Badawi.
The agreement settled the maritime boundaries between the two countries, including their territorial seas, continental shelves, and Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs). It also created a Commercial Arrangement Area for joint oil and gas development, allowing Malaysia to develop certain offshore blocks like Kikeh, while Malaysia recognized Brunei’s claim to Louisa Reef. The agreement also protected the “unsuspendable rights” of Malaysian vessels to pass through Bruneian waters.
On top of this, it set a framework for joint land surveys to permanently demarcate the border between Brunei and Malaysia’s Sarawak region (i.e. Limbang). However, what little progress was made on the Limbang front was undone by Abdullah Badawi when he claimed that by signing the exchange of letters, Brunei had given up its claim on Limbang. Brunei’s then Second Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade Lim Jock Seng publicly denied that Limbang had been discussed and added that the negotiations concerned boundary demarcation generally.
After last month’s meeting with Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, Anwar said that about 50 percent (or 264.791 kilometers) of the Malaysia-Brunei land boundary had been jointly surveyed and demarcated. The two leaders set a target to finish surveying the entire land boundary by 2034, with Sector F-G slated for completion by May 31, 2027, Anwar added.
This is not the only case in which the stroke of a British colonial cartographer divided territories and left newly independent countries to deal with the consequences. The Limbang issue has remained unresolved since the 1870s. But unlike India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars over Kashmir, Brunei and Malaysia have chosen patient diplomacy.
Limbang, instead of becoming a cause of conflict, has become a bridge between the two countries. For residents of Temburong, travelling to Bandar via Limbang has become part of their daily routine. They cross into another country almost as a matter of habit, sometimes without even thinking about the fact that they have to enter Malaysia to reach another part of their own country.
Whenever young Bruneians want to eat chicken wings and drink beer, they often head to Limbang in neighboring Malaysia. It may sound strange to cross an international border for an evening out, but Limbang is only a few kilometers from Brunei’s capital, Bandar Seri Begawan.
One might marvel at how, despite an unresolved border dispute in the area, the two countries allow their citizens to freely travel back and forth. But as part of ASEAN, Bruneians and Malaysians don’t need visas to cross the border.
Geography has also made this sleepy town something of a go-between for Brunei and Malaysia, especially when it comes to Temburong, Brunei’s eastern district. Many people living there travel daily to Bandar Seri Begawan for work, but the land route takes them through Limbang. In effect, to travel from one part of their own country to another, they enter Malaysia and then cross back into Brunei. Limbang residents face a similar peculiarity when traveling within Sarawak, of which Limbang is a part. To reach Miri, the nearest Sarawak city, they have to pass through Brunei before re-entering Sarawak to the west.
For a foreign traveler, the arrangement can be bewildering, as multiple border crossings and immigration stamps can quickly fill up their passports. For Bruneians and Malaysians, it is easier, as they can generally use their identity cards for cross-border travel.
Limbang’s curious status is the result of an unresolved border dispute that dates back to the British colonial era – a dispute that the two sides are now moving toward resolving. During the 27th Annual Leaders’ Consultation in Bandar Seri Begawan on August 21, Brunei’s Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim discussed the demarcation of the two countries’ land boundary. More than half of the border has now been demarcated. Yet the question of Limbang still lingers on.
In a joint communiqué issued after their meeting, the two leaders reaffirmed the 2009 Exchange of Letters, the March 2012 boundary memorandum and its Terms of Reference, collectively describing them as binding instruments. It also directs the two sides to resolve Sector F–G, which covers the Limbang area, solely through the watershed principle, using one jointly determined watershed, before completing the survey and demarcation by May 31, 2027.
According to senior Bruneian journalist Malai Hassan Othman, Sector F–G is supposed to cover roughly 6.6 kilometers from Bebuloh towards a point west of Bukit Gadong, near Kampong Limau Manis and the Kuala Lurah-Tedungan crossing (Kuala Lurah is the Brunei border checkpoint, and Tedungan is the matching Malaysian checkpoint in Sarawak for travel between Brunei and Limbang. It lies along the Brunei-Muara-Limbang frontier and is therefore geographically connected to Limbang. But it would be misleading to describe the sector as synonymous with the entire Limbang territorial question.
Malai Hassan, in an article published on LinkedIn, explained in detail the historical background of the sovereignty dispute over Limbang. Buttressing Brunei’s claim, he writes that records from 1970 clearly indicate that the late Sultan Haji Omar ’Ali Saifuddien, father of the present Sultan, stressed Brunei’s claim over Limbang.
Historically, Limbang was governed within the Brunei Sultanate and provided revenue, food, and river access to the sultanate. However, the Limbang Rebellion of 1884 was a crucial conflict between the Sultanate of Brunei and the indigenous residents of Limbang that led to the annexation of Limbang in March 1890 by Charles Brooke, the rajah of Sarawak. He claimed that local Limbang chiefs no longer wanted the Sultan’s rule and preferred Sarawak.
The British gave tacit and informal approval to the annexation of Limbang despite fierce protests from Sultan Hashim of Brunei.
articles.summary: The territory's curious status is the result of an unresolved border dispute between Malaysia and Brunei that dates back to the British colonial era.

articles.title: Why Pakistan Is Shrugging Off Trump’s Latest Iran Sanctions
articles.full_text:
A Pakistani statement signals to Tehran that Islamabad will not undermine a relationship or existing trade ties that have long faced pressure from U.S. sanctions.
Pakistan’s ambassador to Iran Imran Ahmed Siddiqui and Iranian officials pose for a photograph after meetings at Zahedan on Sep. 1, 2026, aimed at strengthening Pakistan-Iran cooperation in the fields of education, trade, connectivity and border management.
U.S. President Donald Trump last week announced the launch of an extensive new sanctions campaign against Iran. The U.S. government has described “Operation Economic Outcast” as an “economic D-Day” against Iran.
On August 24, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the move an unprecedented effort to sever every remaining economic lifeline that is sustaining the Iranian government. The newly announced sanctions are set to target key sectors, including digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Another part of these sanctions is aimed at warning countries and companies that continue to deal with Iran that they risk exclusion from the U.S. financial system.
The announcement has drawn concern and criticism from several countries that maintain economic ties with Iran and stand to be directly affected by these sanctions threat.
Pakistan’s response to news of the U.S. sanctions against Iran has been measured, signaling that it has little intention of changing its current approach of working with Iran.
Islamabad appears unwilling to subordinate its bilateral economic relationships to Washington’s latest unilateral dictates. The Foreign Office issued a carefully worded statement that can be read less as concern over American pressure and more as a quiet assertion of its policy continuity.
Foreign Office Spokesperson Tahir Andrabi made clear that Pakistan’s trade with Iran rests on international law and the two countries’ bilateral agreements. “About trade with Iran, Pakistan is following international law, and our bilateral trade agreements with Iran,” Andrabi said at the weekly media briefing. “As such, our trade remains in consonance with our obligations.”
The language appears to deliberately prioritize Pakistan’s commitments to Iran over any expectation of compliance with American secondary sanctions. Interestingly, there was no suggestion of a review or suspension of commercial ties between the two countries. At the same time, the foreign office’s emphasis remained on continuity of ties between Pakistan and Iran under existing legal frameworks.
Pakistan’s position reflects a careful balancing act.
On the one hand, it sends a clear signal to Tehran that Islamabad will not undermine a relationship or existing trade ties that have long faced pressure from U.S. sanctions. This stance underscores a commitment to preserving and potentially building new momentum in bilateral engagement with Iran.
On the other hand, Pakistan has avoided directly criticizing the American measures. Instead, it has placed the newly announced sanctions within the broader context of the Iran-U.S. confrontation, which Pakistan is trying to address through its mediatory efforts.
For instance, Andrabi stated that “Pakistan hopes that, as part of a wider settlement of the U.S.-Iran standoff, all economic issues will also be settled in the long run, as they form an important part of a viable settlement.”
“Pakistan remains engaged in its mediatory role in this regard,” he added.
By framing the matter this way, Pakistan effectively declined to address the sanctions as a bilateral problem between itself and Washington. Instead, it positioned itself as a facilitator seeking a comprehensive diplomatic outcome in which trade and economic questions would logically be addressed.
Moreover, Pakistan’s careful response reflects a broader assessment in the international community that the latest U.S. measures reveal more desperation than a well-calibrated approach.
Iran has lived under layers of U.S. sanctions for decades. These also include penalties on foreign companies trading or dealing with Iran. While these restrictions may have constrained Iranian oil exports and imposed painful economic costs on the country, they have not fundamentally altered Tehran’s core positions. The question now is whether a fresh unilateral campaign that lacks the backing of a multilateral body or a clear basis in international law can succeed where previous efforts have fallen short.
According to reports, these new pressure measures could become more consequential if Washington can manage to close the remaining trade channels that have survived earlier rounds of sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran’s immediate neighbors, like Pakistan. However, achieving that outcome appears unlikely.
China has already signaled its firm resistance to the U.S. measures. Its Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian stated last week that Beijing firmly opposes “illegal unilateral sanctions” and will take “all necessary measures” to safeguard its rights and interests. “Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted,” he said.
It is noteworthy that both Pakistan and China have framed their responses around adherence to international law. This shared language effectively denies legitimacy to unilateral U.S. measures that lack United Nations authorization.
Analysts note that such sanctions often function more as rhetorical escalation than as channels capable of producing decisive change on the ground. Their primary cost may ultimately be borne by Washington’s own reputation. This is arguably more true as the gap between unilateral pressure and multilateral consensus has become harder to ignore in the wake of the ongoing Iran-U.S. tensions.
In this context, Pakistan’s position seems measured, and reflects an understanding that these new sanctions are not going to work and that issues with Iran should be addressed via dialogue. Pakistan’s response essentially avoids direct confrontation with the U.S. while quietly aligning itself with a wider international sentiment that questions the efficacy and legality of Washington’s sanctions.
By insisting on the primacy of international law, bilateral agreements, and a comprehensive diplomatic settlement, Islamabad is trying to protect its own economic interests while making sure it doesn’t close the door on its mediatory role between Iran and the United States.

articles.title: As the World Nomad Games Come Home, Japarov Expands Kyrgyzstan’s National Story
articles.full_text:
The opening of the games coincided with Kyrgyzstan’s 35th independence anniversary and a major Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.
A group of tourists pose in Bishkek’s central Ala-Too square on Aug. 31, hours before the World Nomad Games got underway.
Kyrgyzstan marked 35 years of independence in grandiose fashion on August 31. More than 20 world leaders arrived in Bishkek throughout the day ahead of a landmark Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit, before the curtain rose on the sixth World Nomad Games with a glamorous opening ceremony in the evening. 
Considering the games’ moniker as the “Olympics of the nomadic world,” the spectacle more than befit the occasion. It took place at the city’s newly built 51,000-seater Bishkek Arena, the largest stadium in Central Asia, and featured an impressive array of dignitaries, such as Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The event was reminiscent of the 2012 Summer Olympics in London in its blend of national culture, history, and showmanship. 
Including a lengthy pre-show program, the ceremony lasted nearly seven hours. It began with a series of performances by some of the biggest names in Kyrgyz music, young and old. Then came the 18 heads of state, each personally welcomed by President Sadyr Japarov, with every greeting shown on screens around the stadium. 
Then came the Kyrgyz national anthem, a processional roll call of the 104 countries taking part in this year’s games, and a speech by Japarov, who theatrically rose out of the floor via an elevator platform before delivering his remarks. At that point, there were still nearly 2 more hours’ worth of ceremony to go. 
What followed was a vast dramatic journey through Kyrgyz and nomadic heritage, consisting of a succession of dance routines put on by some 3,000 performers and 300 horsemen, and a non-stop background show of glitzy visual effects. 
The show depicted a variety of scenes, from the symbolic collection of water at Issyk-kul to an episode that ominously appeared at first to represent the Mongol invasion of Kyrgyzstan. (However, the would-be conquerors were eventually revealed to be athletes looking for a game of Kok Boru, one of the country’s traditional sports.) 
Altogether, the performance was impressive in its ambition and exhilarating in its execution — and that was before it was capped off with a fireworks show and short concert given by Nicole Scherzinger from the Pussycat Dolls. 
In many ways, the ceremony encapsulated a broader tendency of the games: conceived by Kyrgyzstan’s government in the early 2010s as a way to improve the country’s image abroad, they have also helped refashion its national identity at home.
“Following coups in 2005 and 2010, and that year’s violence in Osh, Kyrgyzstan was most commonly associated with inter-ethnic tensions, conflict, and other negative things,” Dr. Arzuu Sheranova, an independent researcher based in Germany, told The Diplomat.
“Although the government was initially skeptical of the idea, [they realized] eventually that the games could be used to attract foreign investments [and] rebrand the country as a safe destination for foreign tourists,” she explained. 
What followed was a model, if not entirely intentional, case study in nation-building. Because the Kyrgyz government began to emphasize nomadic self-branding so heavily when preparing to welcome an international audience during the Nomad Games in 2014, 2016, and 2018, the campaign ended up having significant knock-on effects domestically.
“20 years ago, nomadic culture was viewed as backwards, generally looked down upon, and, for the government, was not at all a priority,” Sheranova said. “But the emphasis on nomadic and ethnic elements helped fuel a boom in Kyrgyzstan’s fashion industry, and nomadism and ethno-themed culture have since become a movement in both men’s and women’s fashion.”
Eventually, she said, this nomadic identity surpassed the government’s long-standing official vision for the country, Kyrgyz Jarany, or “Kyrgyz citizen,” which promotes a shared civic identity and emphasizes multi-ethnic social co-existence, and makes little mention of nomadic heritage. 
According to Dr. Shairbek Juraev, a political scientist who heads Crossroads Central Asia, an independent research institute based in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Jarany was also born of the Osh interethnic violence in 2010, and is similar to how “Kazakh” is used in neighboring Kazakhstan to refer to ethnic Kazakhs, while “Kazakhstani” denotes citizens of the country more broadly. 
But while Kyrgyz Jarany is supposed to make room for Kyrgyzstan’s national minorities, “such as Uyghurs or Uzbeks,” Juraev said, “it is pretty much dead,” thanks in part to the “turn towards increasing the role of Kyrgyz language” that has taken place under the Japarov presidency. 
Indeed, signs of the cultural phenomena described by Juraev and Sheranova appeared at Monday’s opening ceremony. Many of the locals, who made up the majority of the estimated 29,000 people in attendance, were dressed in ethno-themed clothing in Kyrgyzstan’s national colors, or in both.
In a similar vein, Japarov began his speech by praising Kyrgyzstan’s “past, present and future.” He hailed the convergence of events on August 31 as an appropriate way of both marking 35 years of the country’s independence and “glorifying” the legacy of the “nomadic civilization” created by its citizens’ ancestors. 
Beyond these references to history, however, Japarov’s remarks were more focused on the present. The 10-minute speech featured a catalog of major forthcoming government-supported projects, such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway and the Ala-Too ski resort.
That emphasis on development was fitting, given how the games have served as a deadline for major infrastructure initiatives. The Bishkek Arena, for example, is now Central Asia’s largest stadium, having been completed just days before it hosted the opening ceremony. Similarly, the hippodrome in the lakeside resort town of Cholpon-Ata, which hosts most of this week’s sporting events, has been renovated to accommodate 10,000 spectators. 
Manas International Airport, the country’s largest, has also undergone major reconstruction, while roads around Issyk-kul have been upgraded, including a new 15.64-kilometer, four-lane ringroad around Cholpon-Ata designed to ease congestion.
In this sense, the games have offered Japarov an opportunity to showcase a country being physically transformed under his watch.Juraev and Sheranova say that is no small coincidence, given his plans to participate in Kyrgyzstan’s upcoming presidential elections in January 2027. 
“[Japarov] and his team will make every effort to take advantage of all these big events as an illustration of how well the country is doing when it comes to the campaign later on,” Juraev told The Diplomat. 
“In Kyrgyz culture, people organize feasts when everything is okay, when they are economically stable; it is an indication that everything is good, and only when everything is good can you have a feast,” Sheranova agreed.
“And the games are a feast at the national level — what Japarov’s administration is doing right now is demonstrating the results of his work during his first term,” she said.
