articles.title: The Reason Japan Cannot Commit to Dialogue with North Korea
articles.full_text:
The Tanaka affair has cast a long shadow.
Only two Japan-North Korea summit meetings have ever been held, both between Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi and former North Korean leader Kim Jong Il, in September 2002 and May 2004. Since then, an inter-Korean summit was held in October 2007, followed by three more in 2018. U.S.-North Korea summits were held in June 2018, February 2019, and June 2019. Yet Japan and North Korea have not met at the summit level in over two decades.
What makes summit dialogue uniquely difficult for Japan is the abduction issue. From the 1970s through the 1980s, North Korean agents abducted a large number of Japanese citizens. The abduction of Megumi Yokota, a middle school student at the time, especially shocked Japanese society, and resolving the abduction issue has been declared a “high-priority issue” by every successive administration.
Japanese sanctions on North Korea are the heaviest in the world, yet they have not led to the return of a single abductee to Japan since the five abductees came home in October 2002. Japanese public opinion nonetheless persistently calls for heavier sanctions, driven by anger and distrust. This is despite the fact that it was dialogue, not sanctions, that secured Koizumi’s signal achievement: an apology from North Korean leader Kim Jong Il and the return of five abductees and their family members.
The issue is serious and complex. Even if North Korea were to allow Japanese nationals to return, claiming that “new abduction victims have been identified,” that would not produce unqualified satisfaction on the Japanese side. Distrust toward a country that has long insisted “the abductions have been resolved” would only deepen; and even if ten people were to return, the Japanese public would suspect there may be still more abductees. Japan has struggled for years with the question of what would constitute a “resolution” of the abduction issue, but it proved an impossible task given that human lives were at stake.
The key figure who made Koizumi’s historic visit to North Korea possible was Tanaka Hitoshi, the then Director-General of the Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He conducted nearly thirty secret meetings with the North Korean agent known as “Mr. X,” in China and other third countries. The meetings were so secret that even Shinzo Abe, then Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary, was not made aware of them.
After Kim Jong Il admitted to and apologized for the abductions and the five abductees were returned to Japan, public anger fell not only on North Korea but also on Tanaka. Not all abductees had returned, and it emerged that Tanaka had accepted a North Korean suggestion for a “temporary return” of roughly two weeks rather than permanent residency for the five abductees.
Tanaka likewise attracted Abe’s ire. Having taken a strong personal interest in the abduction issue, Abe could not forgive Tanaka for advancing negotiations without informing him. Tanaka was ultimately summoned to Diet deliberations, where he broke down in tears under withering criticism of how the negotiations had been handled. Despite having acted on the prime minister’s instructions, Tanaka received no defense from Koizumi, perhaps because public opinion was too hostile. Koizumi’s diplomacy toward North Korea deserves a more positive assessment than it has received, and it is regrettable that this episode cast such a long shadow. Tanaka was so thoroughly pilloried by Japanese conservatives as a “traitor” that this once-promising diplomatic ace never became vice-minister for foreign affairs or ambassador to the United States.
The affair had lasting consequences. It taught subsequent administrations that even if they were to seriously pursue North Korea diplomacy, public support would be hard to secure given widespread skepticism toward dialogue, and that even partial success, short of a “full resolution” of the abduction issue, would expose them to harsh criticism regardless.
Having witnessed the keelhauling of Tanaka, even the most talented Foreign Ministry officials will not actively pursue North Korea diplomacy. Japanese civil servants are divided from the moment of hiring into elite “career” and specialized “non-career” tracks, with the hierarchy between the two tracks never reversed. Career diplomats rotate postings every two to three years and are guaranteed advancement if they handle North Korea safely without taking risks. The perverse result is that the most capable diplomats are the least likely to actively pursue dialogue with Pyongyang.
This structural problem must be addressed before Japan can make progress on any of its outstanding issues with North Korea. Ultimately, overcoming the problem requires strong political leadership from the prime minister.

articles.title: Angola Is Emerging as One of Africa’s Most Important Gateways to the Asia-Pacific
articles.full_text:
The story of its success has not been straightforward.
Angola’s city of Lobito, resting behind a natural harbor on the Western side of Africa, is becoming a major industrial port city. It is the second largest port along Angola’s coast, and it has grown steadily over the course of the last two decades, strategically placed as the head point of the internationally funded Lobito Corridor. The story of its success has not been straightforward. The Benguela Railway runs from Lobito into the heart of Africa, bearing critical minerals like cobalt and copper from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. But Angola’s export wealth has only recently turned towards minerals and, in the past, it focused on oil exports from terminals and offshore reserves at Cabinda and Luanda. Oil markets are volatile, and lower global oil prices in 2014 plunged Angola into a severe economic depression, shaking its energy resource-driven economy and paving the way for the diversified market that is developing across Angola today. It is a market uniquely expanding into global trade, and it will be critical for Asia-Pacific energy supplies and trade links in the long run.
Angola has now paid back the majority of its infrastructural loans to China, bringing the peak of total borrowing from $45 billion in 2000 to roughly $12 billion today. Angola has steadily repaid its debt without restructuring, paying off more than necessary during its payment cycles, and showcasing an ‘Angola Model’ of using oil-backed loans which have become uniquely favorable positions in the midst of recent rises in global oil prices. For development loans where oil revenues do not contribute to repayment, Angola has found unique opportunities to readjust repayment plans for fiscal sustainability. For example, the country announced a “debt-for-education” swap with the World Bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency in March of this year. The deal converts debt repayments into investments in education. The savings on interest will be fully applied to an educational program that spans all 21 provinces, aiming to empower girls’ school attendance, human capital, and access to education. The $400 million agreement was finalized in late July, with disbursements to over thirty schools beginning immediately, impacting over 32,000 students.
The debt restructuring is a novel way to continue development even after loans have served their infrastructural purposes, and it represents Angola’s fiscal responsibility, ambitiously aimed at diversifying its own economy. Angola has also stepped up on the world stage. The crisis in the Gulf, which has strangled energy supplies for much of Asia, turned out to become a major opportunity for Angola. For example, President João Lourenço inaugurated a major aluminum plant in Bengo Province in January. That factory now puts out 240 tons of ingots daily, pouring into the 9 percent gap in supplies caused by the closure of Hormuz. Furthermore, Angola’s natural gas reserves are contributing to $2 billion in new investments for an Ammonia-Urea complex, one that, when it opens in 2027, will produce roughly 4,000 tons of fertilizer per day. Angolan trade is not only expanding into novel markets, but traditional markets are also tapping into its supply. Australia, Vietnam, and Hong Kong are likely candidates to increase imports from Angola. The oil sector dominates these new networks; however, they lead to expanded cooperation along the supply chain, especially as Angolan markets build out more value-added industry. These emerging links are particularly significant for the Asia-Pacific, where demand for energy and industrial inputs is reshaping supply chains.
In the case of Vietnam, Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng suggested that cooperation with Angola needed to accelerate, considering Angola’s recent role as Chair of the African Union. He noted, furthermore, that Vietnam would function as Angola’s gateway into ASEAN, seeking multi-layered market integration that can expand beyond bilateral relations. As for other partnerships, China stands out as Angola’s second largest African partner, mostly due to oil exports. South Korea has, like Vietnam, called for new approaches to the Angolan relationship, partly as a response to prioritizing new oil and LNG supply chains following the Gulf crisis. The expansion of the Lobito Corridor is the largest factor in Angola’s new relationships with Asia, and it is expected to be a major driver for diversification across Angola’s and all of Africa’s global trade links. For the Asia-Pacific, this creates a potential bridge between African critical minerals and energy resources and Asian manufacturing, technology, and consumer markets. For the Lobito Corridor specifically, a Memorandum of Understanding between the European Union, United States, and the African Development Bank has already opened the door to significant investment, including cooperation with partners in the East.
President João Lourenço’s leadership has further encouraged economic reforms aimed at improving transparency, strengthening institutions and encouraging private sector growth, each aimed at solidifying and securing international investment interests. Angola’s investment promotion agency has received hundreds of proposals across sectors ranging from agriculture to logistics, manufacturing and tourism. The uptick in economic potential comes as a recognition of Angola’s fiscal stability and its appealing supply of natural resources and strategic geography. The Lobito Corridor makes inland investment possible as well, finally overcoming many of the infrastructure bottlenecks that plagued exports. Minerals flowing from Zambia and the DRC are critical to the world, for low-carbon energy technologies, advanced electronics, and battery storage systems. For Asian economies seeking to diversify critical-mineral supply chains, the corridor offers a potentially important alternative route into Africa’s resource base.
These materials pair with Angola’s existing energy exports, and hydrocarbons still represent a substantial share of GDP; however, policymakers in Luanda are actively sorting out a new model. Alongside oil, natural gas is playing a growing role as a transitional resource, supporting power generation and industrial development while helping to diversify the energy mix. The national energy company Sonangol is also pursuing plans to expand refining capacity, including building a large plant near Lobito. Increasing domestic processing will reduce the reliance on imported fuels while creating skilled jobs and strengthening Angola’s industrial base. Hydropower helps to power this transition domestically, where significant river systems and existing large-scale dams provide plentiful electricity generation for industrialization while improving energy reliability. In a region where power constraints often limit economic activity, renewable energy sources provide the foundation for sustained growth while aligning with a plethora of global efforts aimed at reducing carbon emissions. A resilient energy supply is a necessity for the expansion of cooperation with partners like those in South Korea or Vietnam, as well as for deeper integration with wider Asia-Pacific supply chains.
A stronger Angolan economy, with reliable power and a trustworthy government, will support stability across southern and central Africa by improving trade routes, expanding economic opportunity, and strengthening regional cooperation. The benefits, however, will spread far beyond national borders. None of this means Angola’s challenges have disappeared. Diversifying the economy long dependent on oil takes time, and building institutions that encourage sustained private investment requires persistence and the political will. It requires international trust-building and newfound cooperation with partners like those ready for business in ASEAN. Infrastructure projects like the Lobito Corridor will go a long way, and so will diplomatic agreements, but innovative development financing may go even further as it sows the seeds for a future generation of builders and leaders for a stronger Angola. In many ways, Angola’s debt refinancing through the World Bank substantiates Angola’s economic ambitions in the Asia Pacific and elsewhere. For Asia-Pacific policymakers and investors, Angola’s trajectory offers a case study in how infrastructure, energy diversification, and development finance can reshape a country’s role in global supply chains.
Angola’s city of Lobito, resting behind a natural harbor on the Western side of Africa, is becoming a major industrial port city. It is the second largest port along Angola’s coast, and it has grown steadily over the course of the last two decades, strategically placed as the head point of the internationally funded Lobito Corridor. The story of its success has not been straightforward. The Benguela Railway runs from Lobito into the heart of Africa, bearing critical minerals like cobalt and copper from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. But Angola’s export wealth has only recently turned towards minerals and, in the past, it focused on oil exports from terminals and offshore reserves at Cabinda and Luanda. Oil markets are volatile, and lower global oil prices in 2014 plunged Angola into a severe economic depression, shaking its energy resource-driven economy and paving the way for the diversified market that is developing across Angola today. It is a market uniquely expanding into global trade, and it will be critical for Asia-Pacific energy supplies and trade links in the long run.
Angola has now paid back the majority of its infrastructural loans to China, bringing the peak of total borrowing from $45 billion in 2000 to roughly $12 billion today. Angola has steadily repaid its debt without restructuring, paying off more than necessary during its payment cycles, and showcasing an ‘Angola Model’ of using oil-backed loans which have become uniquely favorable positions in the midst of recent rises in global oil prices. For development loans where oil revenues do not contribute to repayment, Angola has found unique opportunities to readjust repayment plans for fiscal sustainability. For example, the country announced a “debt-for-education” swap with the World Bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency in March of this year. The deal converts debt repayments into investments in education. The savings on interest will be fully applied to an educational program that spans all 21 provinces, aiming to empower girls’ school attendance, human capital, and access to education. The $400 million agreement was finalized in late July, with disbursements to over thirty schools beginning immediately, impacting over 32,000 students.
The debt restructuring is a novel way to continue development even after loans have served their infrastructural purposes, and it represents Angola’s fiscal responsibility, ambitiously aimed at diversifying its own economy. Angola has also stepped up on the world stage. The crisis in the Gulf, which has strangled energy supplies for much of Asia, turned out to become a major opportunity for Angola. For example, President João Lourenço inaugurated a major aluminum plant in Bengo Province in January. That factory now puts out 240 tons of ingots daily, pouring into the 9 percent gap in supplies caused by the closure of Hormuz. Furthermore, Angola’s natural gas reserves are contributing to $2 billion in new investments for an Ammonia-Urea complex, one that, when it opens in 2027, will produce roughly 4,000 tons of fertilizer per day. Angolan trade is not only expanding into novel markets, but traditional markets are also tapping into its supply. Australia, Vietnam, and Hong Kong are likely candidates to increase imports from Angola. The oil sector dominates these new networks; however, they lead to expanded cooperation along the supply chain, especially as Angolan markets build out more value-added industry. These emerging links are particularly significant for the Asia-Pacific, where demand for energy and industrial inputs is reshaping supply chains.
In the case of Vietnam, Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng suggested that cooperation with Angola needed to accelerate, considering Angola’s recent role as Chair of the African Union. He noted, furthermore, that Vietnam would function as Angola’s gateway into ASEAN, seeking multi-layered market integration that can expand beyond bilateral relations. As for other partnerships, China stands out as Angola’s second largest African partner, mostly due to oil exports. South Korea has, like Vietnam, called for new approaches to the Angolan relationship, partly as a response to prioritizing new oil and LNG supply chains following the Gulf crisis. The expansion of the Lobito Corridor is the largest factor in Angola’s new relationships with Asia, and it is expected to be a major driver for diversification across Angola’s and all of Africa’s global trade links. For the Asia-Pacific, this creates a potential bridge between African critical minerals and energy resources and Asian manufacturing, technology, and consumer markets. For the Lobito Corridor specifically, a Memorandum of Understanding between the European Union, United States, and the African Development Bank has already opened the door to significant investment, including cooperation with partners in the East.
President João Lourenço’s leadership has further encouraged economic reforms aimed at improving transparency, strengthening institutions and encouraging private sector growth, each aimed at solidifying and securing international investment interests. Angola’s investment promotion agency has received hundreds of proposals across sectors ranging from agriculture to logistics, manufacturing and tourism. The uptick in economic potential comes as a recognition of Angola’s fiscal stability and its appealing supply of natural resources and strategic geography. The Lobito Corridor makes inland investment possible as well, finally overcoming many of the infrastructure bottlenecks that plagued exports. Minerals flowing from Zambia and the DRC are critical to the world, for low-carbon energy technologies, advanced electronics, and battery storage systems. For Asian economies seeking to diversify critical-mineral supply chains, the corridor offers a potentially important alternative route into Africa’s resource base.
These materials pair with Angola’s existing energy exports, and hydrocarbons still represent a substantial share of GDP; however, policymakers in Luanda are actively sorting out a new model. Alongside oil, natural gas is playing a growing role as a transitional resource, supporting power generation and industrial development while helping to diversify the energy mix. The national energy company Sonangol is also pursuing plans to expand refining capacity, including building a large plant near Lobito. Increasing domestic processing will reduce the reliance on imported fuels while creating skilled jobs and strengthening Angola’s industrial base. Hydropower helps to power this transition domestically, where significant river systems and existing large-scale dams provide plentiful electricity generation for industrialization while improving energy reliability. In a region where power constraints often limit economic activity, renewable energy sources provide the foundation for sustained growth while aligning with a plethora of global efforts aimed at reducing carbon emissions. A resilient energy supply is a necessity for the expansion of cooperation with partners like those in South Korea or Vietnam, as well as for deeper integration with wider Asia-Pacific supply chains.
A stronger Angolan economy, with reliable power and a trustworthy government, will support stability across southern and central Africa by improving trade routes, expanding economic opportunity, and strengthening regional cooperation. The benefits, however, will spread far beyond national borders. None of this means Angola’s challenges have disappeared. Diversifying the economy long dependent on oil takes time, and building institutions that encourage sustained private investment requires persistence and the political will. It requires international trust-building and newfound cooperation with partners like those ready for business in ASEAN. Infrastructure projects like the Lobito Corridor will go a long way, and so will diplomatic agreements, but innovative development financing may go even further as it sows the seeds for a future generation of builders and leaders for a stronger Angola. In many ways, Angola’s debt refinancing through the World Bank substantiates Angola’s economic ambitions in the Asia Pacific and elsewhere. articles.title: Mongolia Hosts COP17, Urging Global Partners to Action on Climate Issues
articles.full_text:
Mongolia wanted to see “a shift from talk to action” at COP17. The results were mixed.
The 17th Conference of the Parties to the U.N Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) was convened in Ulaanbaatar from August 17-28, bringing together 196 country representatives plus the European Union to negotiate action-based measures on several climate challenges facing the world today. This year’s COP17 included segments on finance, water, land and people, and food systems. Parties agreed on a new initiative that includes $1.3 billion in financing, but failed to approve a new financial mechanism to combat drought. 
On August 17, the opening ceremony was attended by Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD Dr. Yasmin Fouad, Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture (and president of UNCCD COP16) Dr. Osama Ibrahim Fakiha, and Mongolia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Battsetseg Batmunkh. The global climate gathering also included a visit by South Korea’s former president, Moon Jae-in, and business leaders from Rio Tinto, Trade Development, Oyu Tolgoi, Asian Development Bank, Global Green Growth Institute, and more. 
Welcoming the guests and opening the COP17 gathering, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor stated: “The greatest change we want to see from COP17 is a shift from talk to action, from targets to implementation, and from commitments to measurable results.” 
As Fouad, the UNCCD executive secretary, put it in an interview with The Diplomat before the gathering: “COP17 comes at a pivotal moment for global action on land… I believe countries will come to Mongolia with a shared understanding that the challenge is no longer understanding the problem – we know what is at stake. The priority now is implementation.”
In the last two weeks, the Mongolian government, civil society, and environmental organizations cooperated with global financial institutions, policymakers, businesses, and environmental scientists to advance solutions to emerging issues facing not just Mongolia but the globe, including desertification, drought, and land degradation. Building on the progress made at COP16 in Riyadh, governments at COP17 aimed to negotiate practical tools, partnerships, and financing mechanisms needed to help countries turn existing plans into action. 
According to the UNCCD, more than 70 countries have now developed national drought plans, compared with only three in 2013 – reflecting growing recognition that drought must be managed proactively rather than only once it becomes a humanitarian and economic crisis. 
Desertification, land degradation, and climate change are all interconnected and demand integrated solutions. In Mongolia, the challenge includes extreme climate fluctuations, such as dzud and drought, as well as loss of water, water pollution due to mining activities, as well as mismanagement of rangelands and pastoralism. The combination of these issues in turn becomes additional hindrance to the country’s development. 
The last two days of COP17 were designated for all 197 parties to come to some sort of an agreement on a mechanism to combat drought. The Asian Development Bank Partnership estimated $355 billion is needed every year to combat land degradation and drought, yet current investment stands at only around $77 billion, leaving an annual financing gap of $278 billion.
Unfortunately, on August 28, last day of the COP17, parties failed to come to an agreement and passed the issue to the next COP gathering. 
One of the main disagreements was whether to establish a new drought protocol initiated by the African Group. The bloc of developed countries – including the European Union, Australia, and the United Kingdom – opposed the establishment of a new drought protocol, preferring to utilize previously agreed multilateral frameworks such as Global Environment Facility and to avoid overlapping agreements. 
While drought – and a financial mechanism to combat drought – posed a challenge for the 197 parties to negotiate, rangeland, pastoralism, and water deserve equal attention. 
One of the most important segments of COP17 was the High-Level Ministerial Meeting and Finance Day, where delegates, multilateral banks, and participating organizations announce strategic commitments and financial mechanisms focusing on specific issues such as land restoration, rangeland preservation, and invigorating environmentally friendly, green growth. 
At the High-Level Ministerial Meeting, Mongolia officially launched the global “Rangelands Flagship Initiative,” which focus on sustainable management and restoration of global pasture lands. The initiative was viewed as one of the most important outcomes of the climate gathering. It will bring together 45 projects across 23 countries, amounting to $1.3 billion in funding, making it the largest investment in the rangelands sector in the history of the UNCCD Convention. 
The financial commitments will be assessed by the implementation of individual projects. Participating governments are expected to consider a new policy framework on rangelands and pastoralists designed to increase long-term investment in sustainable rangeland management and strengthen pastoral livelihoods. The initiative also mentioned the establishment of an Eurasian Center for Climate-Resilient Rangelands in Mongolia.
On August 24, Business for Land Forum and Finance Day brought together government, businesses, and investors looking to invest in regenerative landscapes. The Business Council of Mongolia and the UNCCD signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a Business4Land (B4L) platform and Mongolia Hub. The MoU “aims to link consumption, production, and finance through environmental and social standards, as well as financial products focused on preserving natural capital.” 
Moreover, Mongolia also signed a Host Country Agreement (HCA) with Global Green Growth Institute to strengthen the legal and institutional framework for climate financing and augmenting investment environments for green projects. 
The director of the Protected Areas Policy Department at Mongolia’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, Uranchimeg Tserendorj, stated that for the last 32 years, Mongolia’s Law on Protected Areas has protected land all around the country. The legal framework has allowed the country to protect “20.8 percent of land,” Uranchimeg said. 
Mongolia is also seeking a deeper action-based cooperation with both UNCCD and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands. Mongolia’s Environment and Climate Change Minister Sandag-Ochir Tsend met Ramsar Convention Secretary General Dr. Musonda Mumba, “proposing closer cooperation between the Ramsar Convention and U.N. Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) during Mongolia’s COP17 presidency.”
At COP17, mining giants such as Rio Tinto announced their strategy to contribute to Mongolia’s fight against desertification, water pollution, and restoration of forestry by planting 5,000 hectares of forest, investing in renewable energy for company usage, as well as introducing new technology to replenish groundwater. According to the environmental manager of Oyu Tolgoi, one of Mongolia’s largest mining companies, the firm began paying water pollution fees in 2026, a regular quarterly payment of 150-200 million Mongolian tugrik (roughly $42,000 to $55,000). These practices meant to set an example for other mining giants operating in the country. 
In the last two weeks, global partners gathered in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia to discuss and negotiate an issue that has long been a focus for climate advocates. Mongolia’s hosting of the UNCCD COP17 is viewed as a step up in its global engagement and contribution and commitment to climate change. Considering the country’s own struggle with wetland loss, drought, rangeland and pastoral management, the platform urged global businesses, government, and civil society to take actions to help contribute solve these challenges.

articles.title: Tim Cook’s Dark Legacy in China
articles.full_text:
Cook’s leadership perfected Apple’s production – but Chinese workers paid the price.
On September 1, 2026, Tim Cook will hand over control of Apple to John Ternus. He leaves behind one of the most efficient manufacturing systems in consumer electronics, one he helped build as operations chief from 1998.
In China, Cook leaves a second, but related, legacy: workers on Apple lines toiling 60 hours a week or more, often without a rest day and depending on overtime to cover the basic cost of living.
Ternus will have to decide how to handle both of these realities.
At China Labor Watch, we just completed a new investigation into Apple’s supply chains in China. Our conclusion is not simply that Apple’s compliance system fails to prevent violations. Many of the labor conditions that the report identified are baked into the production model itself.
I once asked a worker on an Apple line at a Foxconn factory what he made of the human rights standards Western countries talk about. He called them Western propaganda. What taught him about America, he said, was not standards on paper but the machine-like pace of Apple’s line and pay he was never sure would arrive.
Since 2006 we have investigated Apple’s suppliers in China, publishing 19 reports. I have come to believe blaming Apple alone would be unfair. Apple’s supply chain in China was built on a trade. China needed foreign capital, technology, and jobs. In return, Western firms got cheap labor and speed built on long overtime and extreme scheduling flexibility.
The Chinese government, Apple, and the supplier factories all bear responsibility for the conditions workers face. But Apple has treated allegations of wrongdoing as a compliance problem, rather than the output of its own production model. 
Apple’s product cycles are fast, and launches send order volumes sharply higher. Suppliers work on thin margins and must deliver enormous volumes quickly. The component prices are set; equipment costs are sunk. There is only one place left to ensure profits: labor costs. Workers’ hours and income become the buffer, absorbing the volatility Apple itself generates.
Apple’s answer has been to police this through a Supplier Code of Conduct, audits, public reporting and worker training. While these steps do have an impact, the overall pattern is clear: individual violations may be corrected, but the same problems return.
In 2019 we found withheld wages at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant. At the same plant, more than half the workforce was on dispatch contracts, far above the legal cap of 10 percent. Apple disputed most of our findings but acknowledged excessive use of dispatch workers. In 2022 thousands at the same plant clashed with police over pay promised at recruitment; Foxconn apologized, blaming a computer input error. In 2025 we found dispatch workers still being used above the legal cap. 
This August we found a full-time assembly worker at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant on a base wage of 2,450 yuan a month, about $363, a little above the city’s legal minimum of 2,350 yuan. To reach 4,200 yuan he has to work 60-hour weeks, totaling roughly 87 hours of overtime a month, against a statutory ceiling of 36.
Raising his base wage by 1,750 yuan, about $260 a month, would let him earn the income he needs on a legal schedule. Even if all 200,000 workers employed at peak operating times received that increase for a full year, the cost would be roughly $620 million – about half of one percent of Apple’s $112 billion in net income in the year to September. 
Clearly, Apple can afford to pay more. The discrepancy, then, points to a deeper issue: labor conditions are not given the same priority as output, speed, and profit margin.
Look at how Apple manages suppliers. Yield rates and delivery deadlines are tracked precisely. Missing them can cost a supplier its orders. A labor violation, by contrast, will just produce another audit. Foxconn went through the 2010 suicides and has gone through one labor dispute after another since. To this day it remains one of Apple’s most important partners. 
Suppliers know exactly which metrics are most important to Apple. 
Apple could have set an enforceable wage floor and made labor conditions matter as much as quality and delivery. It has not. 
China has changed, economically and politically. If Apple wants to keep relying on China as its main production base, maintaining the old model now comes at a higher price in both Beijing and Washington. Apple has been willing to pay that price. It has never paid a comparable price to the people who build its phones. 
As if the suffering of thousands of workers wasn’t enough, there are other costs as well. When the United States preaches labor rights while its most emblematic company leaves Chinese workers dependent on illegal overtime to live, the contradiction erodes the very labor and human rights standards it promotes.
Cook proved Apple can control how an iPhone is made. He never showed that Apple is willing to take responsibility for the welfare of the people who make those phones. For 20 years Apple’s priorities have been consistent: production first, responsibility second.
On September 1, Ternus inherits the manufacturing system Cook helped create – and the unpaid debt to the workers who power that system. Whether the debt is paid will not be recorded in the next Supplier Responsibility Report, but it will show up in how the worker on the line describes America to everyone he knows.

articles.title: Uzbekistan’s Presidential Daughter Just Got a Law of Her Own
articles.full_text:
The new presidential administration law grants its head – Saida Mirziyoyeva – sweeping new powers, and immunity.
Saida Mirziyoyeva on a visit to China in late August 2026, in which she met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and other top officials.
Uzbekistan has finally addressed the “legal gap” in regulating activities of the Administration of the President vis-a-vis other state bodies. At least, this is how the president’s press secretary, Sherzod Asadov, framed a new constitutional law that strengthens the administration’s status, grants lifetime immunity to its officials and extends its outreach. 
The Legislative Chamber passed the Law on the Administration of the President on August 6; the Senate approved it the very next day. There was no public discussion and the body of the law was not disclosed before the president signed it on August 14. 
The administration was launched to “provide information, analytical, organizational and supervisory support for the activities of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan” in 2018, two years after Shavkat Mirziyoyev came to power. In 2018-2022 it was headed by Zaynilobiddin Nizomiddinov, and in 2022-2023 by Sardor Umurzakov.
In that time, Mirziyoyev’s eldest daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, served as a deputy director of the Agency for Information and Mass Communications under the administration in 2019-2020, and as a deputy chairman of the Board of Trustees of the National Fund for Support and Development of Mass Media in 2020-2022.
She started working as head of the Department for Communications and Information Policy of the Executive Office of the Presidential Administration in 2022 before becoming an assistant to the president in August 2023. At the same time, Umurzakov was moved to another position and the head-of-administration post was abolished. In June 2025 the post was re-established, and Mirziyoyeva was appointed as the head of the administration. 
The new law, which consists of four chapters and 34 articles, extends the first daughter’s power. The document establishes that the head of the administration is not elected, but appointed and dismissed by the president himself. The Legislative Chamber’s approval is not required, as it is with the prime minister post. Not only can the administration now “issue mandatory instructions and assignments to heads of state bodies and organizations” (article 7), but punish those who fail at their job with “disciplinary actions,” and even fire them. 
The law also gives Mirziyoyeva control over regional hokims (governors). The administration can monitor the implementation of all presidential orders, organize the legal and administrative process for the president to appoint and dismiss regional governors, and dismiss district and city hokims for breaking the law or any other improper behavior (article 18). The administration can do all of this while having direct access to the database of any government institution (article 7).
Article 19 directly collides with the institutional independence of the judicial system. The article spells out that the administration, a body with no judicial function or independent accountability, “coordinates reforms in the judicial and legal sphere [and] develops proposals for reforming the judicial system.” This essentially means that the presidential administration can take part in shaping the country’s judicial-legal reform directly. 
The administration will also take over the anti-corruption compliance system. Mirziyoyeva will appoint and dismiss “deputies (advisors) of heads of state bodies and organizations at the republican level for compliance and internal control against corruption” (article 21) The Diplomat earlier reported that each government institution now has deputies for compliance and internal control against corruption in all state agencies, which directly report to the presidential administration. This essentially means that people now have to report governmental level corruption cases to a government body that has no mechanisms for accountability, but has its officials guaranteed lifetime immunity against any criminal charge, arrest, or inspection. 
Only Uzbekistan’s prosecutor general can initiate a criminal case against staff of the presidential administration, whose immunity after their departure from a post is to last for five years and any cases related to such staff will be reviewed by the Supreme Court. Meanwhile, officials in the presidential administration, such as its head, now have a lifetime immunity. Some protection also applies to the family members (spouses, children, and parents) of presidential administration officials and staff, extending to privacy of personal and professional life, not legal impunity. 
Beyond these significant changes, the law also grants the head of the presidential administration an automatic appointment as deputy chair of the Security Council and through the Security Council’s Secretariat “ensures the President’s constitutional powers relating to the Armed Forces, defense, mobilization, security, and emergency situations.” Therefore, Mirziyoyeva will be able to exercise authority over the country’s armed forces and national security apparatus. 
The new Law On the Administration of the President sends a couple of important signals. First, it legally codifies what the first daughter has already been doing – exercising power with no accountability or limit. She is not elected by the people but appointed by her father. Second, it establishes in the law a failsafe mechanism in case something happens to the president before his current term runs out. 
Third, Mirziyoyeva is clearly not just the president’s daughter, but is being positioned as a potential successor. Her training days are over. Now she is being trusted with the highest level tasks, with the ability to command almost all government institutions, monitor their actions, and demand accountability at her will, all while having lifelong immunity for her own actions.

In that time, Mirziyoyev’s eldest daughter, Saida Mirziyoyeva, served as a deputy director of the Agency for Information and Mass Communications under the administration in 2019-2020, and as a deputy chairman of the Board of Trustees of the National Fund for Support and Development of Mass Media in 2020-2022.
She started working as head of the Department for Communications and Information Policy of the Executive Office of the Presidential Administration in 2022 before becoming an assistant to the president in August 2023. At the same time, Umurzakov was moved to another position and the head-of-administration post was abolished. In June 2025 the post was re-established, and Mirziyoyeva was appointed as the head of the administration. 
The new law, which consists of four chapters and 34 articles, extends the first daughter’s power. The document establishes that the head of the administration is not elected, but appointed and dismissed by the president himself. The Legislative Chamber’s approval is not required, as it is with the prime minister post. Not only can the administration now “issue mandatory instructions and assignments to heads of state bodies and organizations” (article 7), but punish those who fail at their job with “disciplinary actions,” and even fire them. 
The law also gives Mirziyoyeva control over regional hokims (governors). The administration can monitor the implementation of all presidential orders, organize the legal and administrative process for the president to appoint and dismiss regional governors, and dismiss district and city hokims for breaking the law or any other improper behavior (article 18). The administration can do all of this while having direct access to the database of any government institution (article 7).
Article 19 directly collides with the institutional independence of the judicial system. The article spells out that the administration, a body with no judicial function or independent accountability, “coordinates reforms in the judicial and legal sphere [and] develops proposals for reforming the judicial system.” This essentially means that the presidential administration can take part in shaping the country’s judicial-legal reform directly. 
The administration will also take over the anti-corruption compliance system. Mirziyoyeva will appoint and dismiss “deputies (advisors) of heads of state bodies and organizations at the republican level for compliance and internal control against corruption” (article 21) The Diplomat earlier reported that each government institution now has deputies for compliance and internal control against corruption in all state agencies, which directly report to the presidential administration. This essentially means that people now have to report governmental level corruption cases to a government body that has no mechanisms for accountability, but has its officials guaranteed lifetime immunity against any criminal charge, arrest, or inspection. 
Only Uzbekistan’s prosecutor general can initiate a criminal case against staff of the presidential administration, whose immunity after their departure from a post is to last for five years and any cases related to such staff will be reviewed by the Supreme Court. Meanwhile, officials in the presidential administration, such as its head, now have a lifetime immunity. Some protection also applies to the family members (spouses, children, and parents) of presidential administration officials and staff, extending to privacy of personal and professional life, not legal impunity. 
Beyond these significant changes, the law also grants the head of the presidential administration an automatic appointment as deputy chair of the Security Council and through the Security Council’s Secretariat “ensures the President’s constitutional powers relating to the Armed Forces, defense, mobilization, security, and emergency situations.” Therefore, Mirziyoyeva will be able to exercise authority over the country’s armed forces and national security apparatus. 
The new Law On the Administration of the President sends a couple of important signals. First, it legally codifies what the first daughter has already been doing – exercising power with no accountability or limit. She is not elected by the people but appointed by her father. Second, it establishes in the law a failsafe mechanism in case something happens to the president before his current term runs out. 
Third, Mirziyoyeva is clearly not just the president’s daughter, but is being positioned as a potential successor. Her training days are over. Now she is being trusted with the highest level tasks, with the ability to command almost all government institutions, monitor their actions, and demand accountability at her will, all while having lifelong immunity for her own actions. 
Uzbekistan has finally addressed the “legal gap” in regulating activities of the Administration of the President vis-a-vis other state bodies. At least, this is how the president’s press secretary, Sherzod Asadov, framed a new constitutional law that strengthens the administration’s status, grants lifetime immunity to its officials and extends its outreach. 
The Legislative Chamber passed the Law on the Administration of the President on August 6; the Senate approved it the very next day. There was no public discussion and the body of the law was not disclosed before the president signed it on August 14.
articles.summary: The new presidential administration law grants its head – Saida Mirziyoyeva – sweeping new powers, and immunity.

articles.title: India’s BrahMos at Sea: Implications for South Asian Stability
articles.full_text:
The planned Indian deployment of the BrahMos missile on all of its naval warships has destabilizing implications for the region.
A BrahMos fired from INS Chennai during TROPEX 2017
In May 2025, the confrontation between India and Pakistan was limited to the land and air domains. In the naval domain the two sides took to signaling and positioning but did not engage in active combat. At the start of the conflict, India deployed its naval aircraft carrier INS Vikrant for four days in the Arabian Sea but later moved it back to its base in Karnataka. The Pakistan Navy undertook counter-deployments with an operational offensive-defensive posture. It dispersed its surface combatants, intensified maritime ISR, and moved its coastal missile units into a state of heightened readiness. However, there was no confrontation between the two navies during the crisis. 
However, a few weeks after the announcement of the ceasefire between India and Pakistan, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh visited INS Vikrant and issued a stern warning for Pakistan. He said, “If Pakistan tries anything nefarious again, the opening move might come from our Navy.” 
Since the May 2025 clashes, both states have actively invested in further strengthening the capabilities of their naval forces. Recently, the Indian Navy announced its plan to equip more frontline warships with BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles. The plan is to work toward a fleet-wide integration of the BrahMos weapon system by 2030. 
This development may also increase pressure on Pakistan to take both defensive and offensive measures to maintain naval parity in the region. 
Currently, the Indian Navy operates a diverse range of missiles for anti-ship and land-attack roles. This includes the BrahMos missile deployed across 20 major frontline combatant platforms, the Klub series deployed on Talwar-class frigates, Kh-35E Uran deployed on older systems, and French-made Exocet missiles and American Harpoon missiles on its diesel-electric submarines. However, the BrahMos system has proven its operational relevance for the Indian military after its combat use during the May 2025 crisis. Further integration of the BrahMos would provide India with an indigenous option that can help reduce its reliance on a diverse array of imported missile systems. 
In 2024, the Indian Cabinet Committee on Security approved the purchase of 220 Extended Range (ER) BrahMos missiles for naval ships. The ER-BrahMos has a range of 800 kilometers that can increase the operational space for Indian naval platforms against the Pakistan Navy and also engage coastal targets without getting very close to Pakistan. Moreover, the BrahMos is a supersonic missile with a speed of around Mach 3, reducing the time available for an adversary to detect, identify, and respond to the incoming missile. Also, the precision-strike capability of BrahMos provides a major advantage while targeting moving naval platforms. Because of its indigenous production, range, precision, and speed, the BrahMos has emerged as a major weapon for India and an ideal candidate for deployment across all its naval platforms. 
To achieve its target, the Indian Navy is equipping its older and smaller naval vessels with BrahMos launchers, as evidenced by its replacement of the P-15 Termit with four twin-tube BrahMos launchers on Veer-class corvettes, starting with INS Vidyut. The latest Indian warships including the Nigri-class stealth frigates – INS Udaygiri, INS Himgiri, and INS Mahendragiri –are equipped with eight vertically launched BrahMos missiles. All four Visakhapatnam-class destroyers carry 16 BrahMos missile each. The Indian Navy is also planning to retrofit its older warships with BrahMos systems to achieve system-wide integration. India has also successfully tested the BrahMos missile from an underwater platform, paving way for its integration with diesel-electric submarines. Further, India is developing six highly agile compact missile vessels that can carry eight BrahMos missiles each. These are called next-generation missile vessels. 
These developments have significant implications for Pakistan’s naval strategy and also regional strategic stability. Pakistan is undertaking its own efforts to further strengthen its sea-denial strategy. Pakistan has developed an indigenous anti-ship ballistic missile – P282 SMASH – and integrated them with surface combatants like Zulfiqar-class frigates and Babur-class corvettes. The missile has a range of 350 km. Moreover, it has developed the Harbah subsonic cruise missile and acquired Chinese-imported YJ-83 anti-ship cruise missiles. Pakistan Navy has also tested anti-ship air-launched cruise missiles (ALCM) Taimoor to strengthen its maritime capabilities. 
Pakistan is working on its defense systems by deploying CAMM-ER missiles on Babur-class corvettes and LY-80 missiles on Tughril-class frigates. Both offensive and defensive capabilities developed by Pakistan are designed to maintain operational parity with the Indian Navy. However, there would be certain challenges for Pakistan if India successfully integrates all its naval warships with BrahMos missile systems. This would increase pressure on Pakistan to strengthen its maritime surveillance as India would have a quantitative edge in its missile carrying naval platforms. 
As the naval domain is a possible battlefield for a future crisis between India and Pakistan, these developments can have serious repercussions for regional stability. Any attacks on naval systems and coastal areas carry serious escalation risks in a nuclearized environment. India’s accidental launch of a BrahMos missile in May 2022 showcased a serious problem with command and control of this platform in an environment in which two nuclear weapon states operate. Another major problem with the deployment with BrahMos is that the missile is dual-capable in nature and can carry nuclear weapons. This conventional-nuclear entanglement further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation.
In conclusion, the Indian deployment of the BrahMos missile on all of its naval warships has negative implications for deterrence stability, crisis stability, and arms race stability between India and Pakistan. Increasing the number of mobile platforms capable of conducting long-range precision strikes could create greater pressure for Pakistan to adopt countermeasures, while simultaneously increasing the incentives for pre-emption during a crisis. The combination of BrahMos’s long range, high speed, and dual-capable nature further complicates escalation management between two nuclear-armed states, particularly when the origin and intent of a naval strike may be difficult to determine in real time. The developments risks transforming the Arabian Sea from a domain of signaling and maneuver into a potential trigger for rapid escalation, with consequences extending beyond South Asia to the wider Indian Ocean Region.

articles.title: ‘Latin Poison’: Kazakhstan’s Latinization in Russian Media Discourse
articles.full_text:
In criticizing Kazakhstan’s Latinization effort, Russian media is not defending the Russian language or the Cyrillic alphabet, but the symbolic, ideological, and geopolitical hierarchy of the Russian world.
Kazakh National Railway Office in Almaty. Signage in Latin. Almaty, May 2026.
In July 2025, my feature titled “Scripts and Power: How Russian Media Frame the Latinization of the Kazakh Language” was published in The Diplomat. There, I argued, based on my analysis of over 200 articles, that Russian media views Latinization through a politicized lens and relies on conspiratorial, colonial, and nostalgic narratives in commenting on Kazakhstan’s script reform. 
Shortly after, Russian outlet Ritm Evrazii published a piece, “Latin Poison for Kazakhstan,” as a direct response to my feature. Its author, Vladislav Makarov, discussed “the bewilderment among Russians caused by Kazakh officials’ stubborn desire to ban the Cyrillic alphabet.” Makarov further argued that Moldovan or Azerbaijani cultures have not become known worldwide because of their switch to Latin and that the new alphabet serves to “tie [post-Soviet republics] to their new overlords.” 
This piece does not mean that my feature caused a significant stir in Moscow. Nevertheless, it is interesting evidence of how, in responding to an English-language feature about Kazakhstan’s script reform, Makarov reproduced the same Russia-centric narratives described in the original feature. In his words, Kazakhstan has been “connected to the Russian World for centuries,” thus justifying Russia’s commentary on Latinization.  
The script reform in Kazakhstan, aimed at transitioning the Kazakh language from Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet, has been ongoing since 2017. Among the official reasons for the script change are the intentions to strengthen Kazakh identity and language and to rectify the true Kazakh pronunciation, which was affected by the Soviet-imposed Cyrillic script. Conceived under Kazakhstan’s first president, Nursultan Nazarbayev, Latinization is to be fully implemented by 2031. 
Current President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a cautious approach to Latinization. The latest version of the alphabet was presented in 2021, which shares similarities with the common Turkic alphabet adopted by the Organization of Turkic States in 2024. With less than five years left, the alphabet is yet to be finalized. A recent statement by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education assured that the work to improve the latest alphabet version was underway. 
Latinization is intended for the Kazakh language only. So why does Kazakhstan’s script reform, which does not touch Russian at all, provoke such a strong reaction among Russian media? Makarov’s take on the reform sheds light on how Russia perceives Kazakhstan as part of the Russian world, and following this logic, any change within the Russian world affects Moscow. 
The Russian world can be conceptualized as a socially constructed ideological and geopolitical order, which Russia uses to foster belonging, political loyalty, and hierarchy. It rests on the understanding that what unifies the Russian world are the Russian language, the Cyrillic alphabet, and shared history. Its proponents argue that the Russian world is a diverse community representing a multitude of cultures, with Russia holding a legitimately central position. 
The Russian world is not a fixed construct and can be adjusted to align with Moscow’s political motivations. It is often juxtaposed with the Western world, portrayed as a civilization in decline. In practice, Moscow uses the Russian world at a variety of levels. One such use is the Russian World Foundation, a state-run institution primarily aimed at promoting and expanding the Russian language, literature, and culture abroad, particularly in Central Asia. Conceptually, Russian media employ the Russian world notion to perpetuate the ideas of Russia’s symbolic and civilizational power. 
My analysis of 77 articles covering Latinization published between 2001 and 2025 by both mainstream (such as Gazeta.Ru, Lenta.Ru, Kommersant) and fringe nationalist outlets (Regnum, Ritm Evrazii) shows how Russian media instrumentalizes the Russian world to engage discursively with the Kazakh alphabet reform. 
Latinization as a Tool to Exit the Russian World
Kazakhstan’s portrayal as a legitimate and natural part of the Russian world is foundational in Russian media coverage of Latinization. Kazakhstan’s presupposed membership in the Russian world enables Russian outlets to present Latinization as a tool Astana is using to exit this transnational civilizational community. Headings such as “Non-Russian World: Kazakhstan is replacing its ‘big brother’” or “Passive defense against the ‘Russian World’” illustrate how Russian media interprets Latinization as a threat to the Russian world’s integrity. The alphabet reform is argued to have the potential to erode the “common cultural space,” which is one of the “invisible links tying together the CIS countries.” The CIS refers to the Commonwealth of Independent States, an intergovernmental organization formed following the dissolution of the Soviet Union that counts among its members most, though not all, of the former Soviet republics.
At the same time, the idea of the Russian world is fused with both the imperial and Soviet past, demonstrating the concept’s flexible nature, and this fusion has a variety of effects. First, as discussed in a 2021 article published by Lenta.Ru, Kazakhstan’s very existence is portrayed as an outcome of Soviet politics, since it was the Bolsheviks “who turned Kazakhs into a nation and gifted them a state.” According to the article, Kazakh “statehood, culture, and script were all created in Moscow.” This framing of Latinization not only links Kazakhstan’s nationhood to the Soviet regime but also presents the alphabet reform as a sign of ingratitude to Moscow, which perceives itself as a successor of the Soviet Union. 
In another Lenta.Ru article, from 2017, the authors expressed frustration with how Kazakh history books critically approach the Soviet past, one of the outcomes of which was the devastating famine of the 1930s, claiming the lives of over 1.5 million people (one-third of the ethnic Kazakh population of that period). They labeled Latinization as a “symbolic distancing from Russia’s legacy in Kazakhstan,” signs of which they also see in changing the Soviet geographical names to Kazakh. Hierarchical narratives can be observed in a 2017 Vedomosti article, which calls Russia “a metropole,” from which post-Soviet countries are trying to separate out of fear of being “swallowed by the ‘Russian world.’”  
Within the Russian world framework, the Russian language holds a central position and serves as a link that ties Kazakhstan to this transnational community. The Russian language is inseparable from Cyrillic, which Russian media treat not as a mere script but as a symbolic and visual representation of the Russian world. In presenting Latinization as a threat to both the Russian language and its alphabet, Russian media follow the mechanism that scholar Lara Ryazanova-Clarke defined as an “inverse transnational pride.” This mechanism explains that Moscow treats the Russian language as a shared transnational commodity benefiting a majority of communities across the Russian world. These narratives change once a foreign government starts implementing policies that Russia perceives as hostile, which shifts the perception of Russian from a shared commodity to an object requiring Moscow’s protection. 
The idea that Latinization is threatening the Russian language and Cyrillic is present across the pieces analyzed. Kazakhstan’s alphabet reform is called “an offensive against the Russian language and Cyrillic” in several articles, and the choice of this specific militaristic term aims at equating Latinization with a military operation against the Russian world’s most valuable commodity. Such an offensive is reported to cause an outmigration of ethnic Russians from Kazakhstan, thus drastically altering the country’s demography. Moreover, Latinization is expected to split “the Kazakh nation into two parts” since there will be people refusing to consume information in Latinized Kazakh who will turn to Russian. 
Media call Latinization “a problem for Russia” and view the reform as a broader trend toward the worldwide decline of the Russian language. At the same time, Russian media frames Latinization’s negative impact on Russian as affecting the Kazakh language as well. To support this assumption, Russian media introduce a linguistic hierarchy, whereas they present Russian as superior and more resourceful compared to Kazakh, which is portrayed as subordinate. Kazakh and languages of other post-Soviet countries are called “colloquial in nature,” with Russian media claiming that it would be impossible for scholarship in these countries to develop without a proper proficiency and use of Russian, which provides access to global knowledge. Interestingly, this assumption seems to be internalized by Kazakhs as well, as a Regnum article in 2017 quoted famous Kazakh publicist and writer Seydakhmet Kuttykadam stating that “the Kazakh language and literature will fade away without its donor-language,” which is Russian.  
Equally, Russian media securitize Latinization’s impact on Cyrillic. Latinization is called “terrible news for Russia” because it will no longer be able to “formulate cultural codes” through the alphabet, meaning that Kazakhstan will drift further toward the West. Such narratives help us understand how Russian media view Latinization not as a linguistic reform but as a geopolitical reconfiguration impacting Russia’s standing as a regional superpower. In discussing alleged effects of Latinization on Russian and Cyrillic, authors rarely discuss the practical implications of the new alphabet but rather defend the hierarchical and symbolic order created by Russia and perpetuated through the Russian world notion.  
Another salient theme present in the Russian media is Latinization’s framing as administered externally by the Western powers or Turkiye. Through such narratives, it becomes more evident how Russian media contrasts the Russian world with competing civilizational entities. 
This theme relies heavily on conspiratorial language. For instance, coverage by KM.Ru in 2010 claimed that the planned alphabet change means “preparations for a transformation of public consciousness to adapt it to European civilizational standards.” Similarly, Nezavisimaya Gazeta in 2021 referred to “Anglo-Saxons” who, through imposing the Latin alphabet, want to gain “total control over defeated and enslaved peoples.” 
Turkiye, on the other hand, is seen as a greater civilizational competitor, since it offers Kazakhstan kinship based on Turkic identity, culture, and religion. Media portray Latinization as an outcome of Turkiye’s interference in the internal affairs of Russia, communicated through such headings as “Turkiye is displacing Russia in the post-Soviet space” and “A yatagan in the back. Turkiye is edging ever closer to Russia’s borders.” There seems to be awareness in Russian media that between Turkic and post-Soviet identities, Kazakh people might prefer the former. 
Makarov, in his 2025 Ritm Evrazii piece, asked, “Will the Latin alphabet bring the Kazakhs closer to the Turkic world they consider their own? But would a Turk from Istanbul really feel closer to a Kazakh than a Russian from Chelyabinsk?” In asking these questions, he assumed that Latinization was developed in Astana to draw Turkiye and Kazakhstan closer. Such questions are intended to emphasize proximity between Kazakhstan and the Russian world, which is natural and historical, unlike Kazakhstan-Turkiye relations, which are, in this view, politically manufactured rather than based on genuinely shared culture. 
Externalization of Latinization indicates that Russian media view Kazakhstan as subjugated either to the West or Turkiye. Such subjugation is branded as inappropriate and malicious, as these powers seek to meddle in Kazakhstan’s affairs through Latinization. At the same time, the hierarchical positioning of Kazakhstan in relation to Russia is also subjugated in nature, even though never explicitly named as such or criticized. Instead, it is portrayed as beneficial and legitimate. 
The outcome of such rhetoric is that Russian media strips Kazakhstan of any agency in carrying out its domestic linguistic reform. By presenting Latinization as a plot by Western or Turkish powers, Russian media negate Kazakhstan’s sovereign decision to reform the alphabet for the Kazakh language on account of its own interests and aims. 
Makarov’s article was never about Cyrillic or Latin. It was about the anxiety across the Russian media over Kazakhstan’s distancing from the hierarchy Makarov and other authors assume to be natural. Readers familiar with Russian foreign policy will not be surprised by the imperial narratives Russian media produce in relation to the Russian world, the Russian language, and Cyrillic. What might be surprising is that such narratives are activated by the script reform intended for the Kazakh language. 
At the same time, among the fear-mongering articles about the destructive consequences of Latinization, there are rarely concrete examples of why the reform would impact Russian and Cyrillic. Instead, Russian media primarily focus on the superiority of the Russian language and its alphabet and on delegitimizing Latinization as an externally driven project by foreign actors. In the end, Russian media is not defending the Russian language or the Cyrillic alphabet, but the symbolic, ideological, and geopolitical hierarchy of the Russian world.     
This feature is based on the author’s ongoing doctoral research on Kazakhstan’s script reform. All data and analysis are from the author’s original corpus and critical discourse analysis. Quotes are translated from Russian to English.
